meaning_mnemonic: Lying on the <radical>ground</radical> is something that looks just like the ground, the number <kanji>One</kanji>. Why is this One lying down on the ground?
reading_mnemonic: As you're sitting there next to <kanji>One</kanji>, holding him up. One starts to scratch himself. Seems like he was on the floor scratching himself because he was <reading>itchy</reading> (いち).
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Alone</kanji> is <reading>ひと</reading>り. Occasionally, it <reading>eats</reading> (いつ) at you. But you enjoy your free time.

-<kanji>One Thing</kanji> is <reading>ひと</reading>つ.

meaning_mnemonic: Lucky for you (as is the case with many of the lower-stroke kanji), this kanji is the same as the radical you've already learned. The radical that makes up this kanji is <radical>seven</radical> and the kanji (which is exactly the same) is also <kanji>seven</kanji>. So, if you know the radical, you know the meaning of the kanji as well.
reading_mnemonic: You know this kanji means <kanji>seven</kanji>, so let's use that to remember the reading too. <kanji>Seven</kanji> is a lucky number, usually, but this time it isn't so good<kanji>Seven</kanji> percent is all she got on her test after <reading>she chea</reading>ted (しち) on it.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Seven Things</kanji> is <reading>なな</reading>つ. These are your <reading>Nana</reading>s (なな), your grandmas, cloned. Just think, "It's lucky to have seven nanas. They can all cook my favorite foods for me!" What's more, you have one nana for every day of the week, so you'll get your favorite food every day.

-<kanji>Seventh Day</kanji> is <reading>なの</reading>か. You've been stuck inside working for seven days and today you finally have a day off. Your friend asks you if you want to go for a drive but you say, "<reading>Nah, no car</reading> today" (なのか), because you want to relax.

meaning_mnemonic: This kanji is made up of the ground radical (which also happens to be the kanji for "one") and the radical for two. Combine <radical>one</radical> and <radical>two</radical> together and what do you get? <kanji>Three</kanji>!
reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Three</kanji> is the number of chances you get with <reading>San</reading>ta-san (さん). He has a list, and when you get to three "naughty things" lines, that's it. You're on Santa-san's three strikes and you're out list.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Three Things</kanji> is <reading>みっ</reading>つ. The three things that you have are actually three versions of yourself. "Who is the real one?" you ask yourself. "It's <reading>me</reading>!" "Wait, no, it's me!" Just remember that there are three of you, and they're all saying "me me me me me" to try and prove that they're the real you.

-<kanji>Third Day</kanji> is <reading>みっ</reading>か.

kunyomi: うえ, あ, のぼ, うわ, かみ
meaning_mnemonic: You find a <radical>toe</radical> on the <radical>ground</radical>. It's weird, because it's <kanji>above</kanji> the ground, not where toes belong.
reading_mnemonic: Of course when you find a toe <kanji>above</kanji> the ground, you want to know where the toe came from. When you examine it, you see a name written on there. This toe belongs to the local clumsy farmhand, <reading>Joe</reading> (じょう).
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Above</kanji> you is a huge weight. You're holding it up and struggling (it's heavy!). You look up and try to crane your neck to see how much it <reading>weigh</reading>s (うえ), but you can't see the numbers on the side of it. How long can you hold it above your head like this?

When you want <kanji>to lift something</kanji>, you always shout "<reading>Ah</reading> (あ)!" to get the extra power you need. Especially when you want to lift something over your head. Go ahead, try it now. Lift something up and shout "Ah!" Makes you feel powerful, right?

上げる (<kanji>To Lift Something</kanji>) vs. 上がる (<kanji>To Go Up</kanji>).

上る (のぼる) - You want <kanji>to climb</kanji> the mountain, but a gruff old man grabs your shoulder and says "<reading>No bo</reading>y (のぼ), you ain't climbing that thing, not today." The weather isn't good for safety today, so try again later.

上唇 (うわくちびる) - The above lip is the upper lip. The reading for 上 is a bit weird, it's <reading>うわ</reading> instead of うえ. It's almost like うえ, just a little different.

kunyomi: した, さ, くだ, お, しも, もと
meaning_mnemonic: There's the <radical>ground</radical>, and there's a <radical>toe</radical> just <kanji>below</kanji> it. Yep, you know this means "below" because the ground has a toe below it in this kanji.
reading_mnemonic: You keep digging in the ground for the toe <kanji>below</kanji>, but instead you hit something hard and metallic. You try to dig around it, but it's huge. Turns out it's a <reading>car</reading> (か). Keep digging until you unearth the car below. (Inside, you find the toe you were looking for.)
extra_reading_mnemonic:
What's <kanji>below</kanji> you? What's below your foot? Oh no. The worst thing possible: It's <reading>した</reading>.

You want <kanji>to lower something</kanji>. In this case, it's a tree, so you need a <reading>saw</reading> (さ). Lower the tree to the ground gently while you slowly saw it down!

下げる (<kanji>To Lower Something</kanji>) vs. 下がる (<kanji>To Get Lower</kanji>).

下りる (おりる) - You're stuck on a huge mountain, and the only way <kanji>to go down</kanji> is by using your <reading>o</reading>bi (お). So you'll have <kanji>to descend</kanji> this entire mountain with nothing but your obi, acting as a rope. You scream, "<reading>OHHHH</reading>! (お)". Good luck!

You might notice that this is similar to 下る (<reading>くだ</reading>る), and you can use either to describe going down a mountain. The difference is that 下る implies a gradual sloping motion, like floating down a stream, whereas you'd say 下りる if you’re jumping out of trees!

下さい (ください) - <kanji>please</kanji>, <reading>could I</reading> (くだ) have this thing? Pretty please, could I have it?

meaning_mnemonic: Nice! This kanji is the same as the radical that looks just like it (down to the meaning, even!). The radical is <radical>nine</radical> and the kanji is <kanji>nine</kanji>, making the meaning of this kanji really easy to remember as long as you know the radical first.
reading_mnemonic: When you were <kanji>nine</kanji> your favorite foods were <reading>coo</reading>kies (く) and <reading>cu</reading>cumbers (きゅう). Yum yum!
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Nine Things</kanji> is <reading>ここの</reading>つ. The nine things you have are <kanji>nine</kanji> <reading>cocono</reading>ts (ここの). As you can guess from the spelling, coconots are not coconuts. Think of them as… fake coconuts. 

-<kanji>Ninth Day</kanji> is <reading>ここの</reading>か.

meaning_mnemonic: The kanji <kanji>two</kanji> and the radical <radical>two</radical> are the exact same things. Therefore, you know the kanji for two already!
reading_mnemonic: How do you count to <vocabulary>two</vocabulary>? Just use someone's <reading>knee</reading> (に), and then their other knee. There — two knees!
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Two Things</kanji> is <reading>ふたつ</reading>. Emphasis on the <reading>ふた</reading>.

-<kanji>Two People</kanji> is <reading>ふたり</reading>. Emphasis on the <reading>ふた</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: Remember how the radical version of this kanji meant <radical>person</radical> because it looks like a person with their arms down and their legs spread out? Well this is a <kanji>person</kanji> too!
reading_mnemonic: One <kanji>person</kanji> is a <reading>nin</reading>ja (にん) and complained about the new <reading>jean</reading>s (じん) policy. It's harder to more fast with jeans, he argues.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Person</kanji> is <reading>ひと</reading>. People generate a lot of body <reading>heat</reading> (ひと). 

Rarely, a <kanji>person</kanji>'s entire value is based on their <reading>toe</reading> (と).

meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for <radical>enter</radical> first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means <kanji>enter</kanji> as well.
reading_mnemonic: Turns out, after you <kanji>enter</kanji> the tent (remember how the person in the radical is entering one?), you're given a <reading>new</reading> (にゅう) one! Why? No idea, but hey — it's new!
extra_reading_mnemonic:
入る (はいる) - When you want <kanji>to enter</kanji> the room, what do you do? You say "<reading>Hi</reading>" (はい) to everyone to the point of absurdity. "Hi there. Oh hi Frank. Oh hi there Susan. Oh hi there lamp."

入れる (いれる) - When you want <kanji>to insert</kanji> your hand into a hole, an <reading>ea</reading>gle (い) flies out out screaming: "い!" This is something that happens every time you insert your hand into something: an eagle comes out. You don't know why.

meaning_mnemonic: This isn't exactly the same as the <radical>fins</radical> radical, but it's close. Sometimes this will happen (where we have to use a slightly "modified radical" version of the original), so it's good to understand that now, early on. In this case, we have fins. How many fins? <kanji>Eight</kanji> fins. How do you know that? Because you caught four fish with two fins each.
reading_mnemonic: After you count and smell all <kanji>eight</kanji> of your fins, it's time to put them away. You open a large <reading>hatch</reading> (はち) and put them in. This is where you keep your fins, always putting in eight at a time because that's what the boss wants.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Eight Things</kanji> is <reading>やっ</reading>つ. You say <reading>Yah</reading> (や) <kanji>eight</kanji> times for good luck.

-<kanji>Eighth Day</kanji> is <reading>よう</reading>か. You also eat <reading>yo</reading>gurt (yogurt) <kanji>eight</kanji> times for good luck. You say yah and eat a bite of yogurt in succession.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical and the meaning of this kanji are the same. Both are <kanji>power</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic: Who has the most power of anyone? It's the <kanji>Power</kanji> Rangers. They are battling their arch enemy <reading>Ricky</reading> (りき). They defeat him and <reading>lock</reading> (りょく) him up, so that he can't hurt anyone ever again.
extra_reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Power</kanji> is <reading>ちから</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: This <radical>cross</radical> is the symbol for the number <kanji>ten</kanji>. A good way to remember this is to think about all the religions that have crosses and also important sets of tens.
reading_mnemonic: This cross in particular has <kanji>ten</kanji> <reading>jew</reading>els (じゅう) on it. Two on each arm and two in the middle. That's ten jewels!
extra_reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Tenth Day</kanji> is <reading>とお</reading>か. This marks the tenth day since this <reading>talker</reading> (とおか) began talking non-stop. Talkers love talking, but this one is getting quite unbearable… Ten days of talking, can you believe it?

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>mouth</radical> radical and the <kanji>mouth</kanji> kanji are exactly the same!
reading_mnemonic:
Do you remember seeing the construction worker こういち earlier in the 工 mnemonic? If you haven't yet, not to worry!

For kanji with こう readings (there are a lot of them!) we will use the character こういち every time. He's one of the people who started this website, so we'll do our best in the mnemonics to embarrass him as much as possible. Anyways, remember that whenever you see こう, think こういち.

Everyone agrees, the <kanji>mouth</kanji> is <reading>こう</reading>いち's best feature. You stare at it lovingly as he whispers sweet kanji readings to you.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Mouth</kanji> is <reading>くち</reading>. With your <kanji>mouth</kanji>, make a "<reading>kuchi</reading> kuchi kou" (くち) sound.

こういち likes to use his mouth to eat <reading>coo</reading>kies (く). Yum!

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>big</radical> radical and the <kanji>big</kanji> kanji are exactly the same!
reading_mnemonic: There's this <kanji>big</kanji> guy (that's how you remember the radical, remember?), and he's wearing a huge <reading>Tie Dye</reading> (たい, だい) shirt. Because he's so huge, the tie dye shirt is also super huge. Everything about him is pretty big, but the tie dye stands out more than anything.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 大きい (<reading>おお</reading>きい) - What do you do when you see something really, really <kanji>big</kanji>? You say <reading>おお</reading> because you can't believe your eyes.

onyomi: じょ, にょ, にょう
meaning_mnemonic: The radical for <radical>woman</radical> and the kanji for <kanji>woman</kanji> are exactly the same.
reading_mnemonic: When you think of a <kanji>woman</kanji>, think of <reading>Jo</reading>-Anne (じょ), though she usually goes by just "Jo."
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Woman</kanji> is <reading>おんな</reading>. 

Think about how this <kanji>woman</kanji> is <reading>onna</reading> (おんな) roll. She's winning left, right and center. She's unstoppable. Yep, she's truly onna roll!

女神 (めがみ) - This goddess has the most beautiful <reading>目</reading> (め) you've ever seen. You can't stop staring into them. This must be how people know they've met a god.

This reading doesn't happen too often, but if a <kanji>woman</kanji> says "<reading>NOOO</reading>" (にょ) or "<reading>NYOOOOOO</reading>! (にょう)", she really means it so give her some space.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>mountain</radical> radical and the <kanji>mountain</kanji> kanji are the same.
reading_mnemonic: Think about <kanji>mountains</kanji> talking to each other, calling each other by their names and adding the Japanese name-ender <reading>san</reading> (さん) to each of their names. "Hello, Everest-<reading>san</reading>." "Oh hi, Fuji-<reading>san</reading>."
extra_reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Mountain</kanji> is <reading>やま</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>river</radical> radical and the <kanji>river</kanji> kanji are the same as each other!
reading_mnemonic: You're standing next to a <kanji>river</kanji> that's actually used as a <reading>ca</reading>r <reading>wa</reading>sh (かわ). The river washes them all clean.
extra_reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>river</kanji> is used for car washes and to clean <reading>cen</reading>taurs (せん).

meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>construction</radical> radical and the <kanji>construction</kanji> kanji are the same!

This kanji also means <kanji>industry</kanji>, which is what construction is, if you think about it. It's all part of the construction industry.
reading_mnemonic:
Every time a kanji uses the こう reading (there are a lot!), we'll use the character こういち. He's one of the people who started this website, so we'll do our best in the mnemonics to embarrass him as much as possible. Like this:

You see some <kanji>construction</kanji> in front of you. There, standing shirtless (only suspenders and a hard hat) is <reading>こう</reading>いち, looking back at you.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 飴細工 (あめざいく) - Rarely, こういち wants to eat (sugar sculptures) by making them into <reading>coo</reading>kies (く)!

other_meanings: Repetition, Reduplication, Iteration Mark, Kanji Repeater, Repeater Kanji
meaning_mnemonic:
This is a strange kanji because it doesn't really mean anything at all. In fact, what it does is it repeats the kanji that comes before it. For example: 人々 is actually 人人. This kanji shows up whenever there's a repeating kanji, because it's often easier to write than writing a more complicated kanji twice. That's why this kanji is the <kanji>repeater</kanji>. It repeats what comes before it.

To remember that this kanji is the repeater, though, think of a <radical>prison</radical> with <radical>drop</radical>s of water dripping over and over in it. Drip drop drip drop. It does that over and over again, driving the prisoners nuts. But it never stops. It just repeats over and over.
reading_mnemonic:
This symbol doesn't really have a name, but it's sometimes called the のま because it looks like the katakana characters ノ and マ put together. If you know katakana then this will be easy to read. If you don't, think of it this way:

Your mom is the <kanji>repeater</kanji>. She is trying to feed you over and over again. You're full today, so maybe tomorrow. You keep yelling "<reading>No ma</reading> (のま)!" but she doesn't stop. She's on a repeating track, never stopping, repeating forever.

meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the radical that look like this are exactly the same. They are both <kanji>street</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic:
So you're walking down this <kanji>street</kanji>, and off in the distance you see the silhouette of somebody. A lady. Big, black curly hair and red eyes. It is the street-woman, Mrs. <reading>Chou</reading> (ちょう).

In general, Mrs. Chou is a mean, evil woman, so as long as you imagine her within those parameters, you're good. And, when I say she is a "street-woman" in the mnemonic, I don't mean she is homeless. She has a nice, middle-class home that's not outside of her financial means. What I'm saying is she wanders the streets looking for evil things to do. These are HER streets.
extra_reading_mnemonic: Mrs. Chou is angry at the <kanji>street</kanji> lined up with <reading>ta</reading>ter (てい) tots. People are happy how you can eat from them as you walk along, and she doesn't like happy people.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical <reading>middle</reading> and the kanji <kanji>middle</kanji> are both the same. So if you know one, you know the other.
reading_mnemonic:
To remember the reading for this kanji, we use the word Chewbacca to pull up ちゅう in our memory.

If you remember back to the radical 中, a stick was stuck in the middle of the mouth of something. Let's say it was your mouth, and when you look up to see who did it, there stands <reading>Chew</reading>bacca. He's even doing his Chewbacca yell. And it isn't a stick in your mouth, it's an arrow from his bowcaster. It just so happens Chewbacca's bowcaster looks just like this kanji too. Go figure.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Inside</kanji> is <reading>なか</reading>. 

There's a sound coming from <kanji>inside</kanji> the wall. It sounds like a knock, knock, knock noise. You break down the wall, and there's some creepy dude standing inside. He is the <reading>knocker</reading> (なか).

meaning_mnemonic: What's something with <radical>nine</radical> sides? Just add a <radical>drop</radical> and you'll have something that's almost a <kanji>circle</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic:
Do you know about the adorable cat Maru? If not, you should check it out (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z_AbfPXTKms). May seem like a distraction, but if you come back knowing the reading for this kanji, then it's totally worthwhile.

When you think about a <kanji>circle</kanji>, think about <reading>Maru</reading> all rolled up in a little circle, being super adorable. Don't tell me it doesn't melt your heart just thinking about it.

Alternatively, you could also look at this kanji and think of Maru inside of a box, with his little tail sticking out of it. Whatever works best for you, just get yourself to "Maru."
extra_reading_mnemonic: <reading>Gan</reading>dhi (がん) also likes <kanji>circle</kanji>s. Full circles. You see Gandhi chilling with Maru the cat.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>five</radical> radical and the <kanji>five</kanji> kanji are the same.
reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Five</kanji> is the number of buildings <reading>Go</reading>dzilla (ご) will knock down. Oh, look! There he goes now.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Five Things</kanji> is <reading>いつ</reading>つ. You need to <reading>eat</reading> (いつ) them. Just imagine having <kanji>five</kanji> delicious things to eat, sticking each on one finger of your hand.

-<kanji>Fifth Day</kanji> is <reading>いつ</reading>か.

meaning_mnemonic: You open a <radical>lid</radical> and see fish <radical>fins</radical>. You count and there are <kanji>six</kanji>!
reading_mnemonic:
Whenever we need to remember the reading ろく we just use the word <reading>rock</reading>.

You take these <kanji>six</kanji> fish fins and put them on to decorate your drum sticks. This looks good for your <reading>rock</reading> (ろく) and roll concert.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Six Things</kanji> is <reading>む</reading>っつ. You count <kanji>six</kanji> cows. The reason it's six is because you heard exactly six <reading>moo</reading>s (むっ). No more, no less.

-<kanji>Sixth Day</kanji> is <reading>む</reading>か. On the sixth day of the week, you've finally get a break to relax. You arrive at your roadtrip's destination.. You get out of your car and tell it, "<reading>Muy</reading> (むい) bien car (か), muy bien!".

meaning_mnemonic: Here we have a <radical>head</radical> with a <radical>lid</radical> in it, near the top. Imagine the top of someone's head being closed by a lid. Open that lid up and peer inside... it's full of <kanji>yen</kanji> coins, the currency of Japan. Jackpot! And all those yen coins have a nice <kanji>round</kanji> shape, naturally.
reading_mnemonic: What does the word <kanji>yen</kanji> sound like? It sounds like <reading>えん</reading>. Why? because back in the day, Japanese used to have a "ye" sound, but now it doesn't. Instead, it's an "e" sound, which is why yen = えん!
extra_reading_mnemonic:
円 means both "yen" and "round" but in this case we're looking at the round one (because something isn't going to be "yenny"). The adjective version of round is <kanji>round</kanji> or <kanji>circular</kanji>. Just like a yen coin, this "round" is a flat round. As in, if you draw a circle on a piece of paper, you could use this word. Same goes with yen, which is why "yen" and "round" both use the same kanji.

Similarly to 丸, they share the same <reading>まる</reading> reading.

meaning_mnemonic: There are two <radical>mountains</radical> in front of you... and probably a bunch more around you too. You are in a pass, and don't know how to get out. You are frantically looking for the <kanji>exit</kanji> before you freeze to death. The most important thing is to find the exit from this mountain range - your life depends on it.
reading_mnemonic: As you're trying to <kanji>exit</kanji> this mountain range, you suddenly realize that someone is actually hunting you. What?! Then, you find the exit and run towards it. Sadly, the hunter is waiting there, and he <reading>shoots you</reading> (しゅつ). WTF?!
extra_reading_mnemonic:
出す (<reading>だ</reading>す) - <kanji>To Take Out</kanji>.

出る (<reading>で</reading>る) - <kanji>To Exit</kanji>.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical and the meaning of this kanji are almost the same! The radical is <radical>sword</radical>, but we're learning Japanese, so can you name a Japanese <kanji>sword</kanji>? That's right, the most common is a <kanji>katana</kanji>, which happens to be the meaning of this kanji as well.
reading_mnemonic: So now you have this sweet <kanji>katana</kanji> in your hands and you're swinging it around like an idiot. Feel free to make whooshing noises as you swing it around. To become a master katana wielder, you decide to travel to <reading>とう</reading>きょう (Tokyo). とうきょう has the best sword and katana schools in the world, so it makes sense to travel to とうきょう.
extra_reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Sword</kanji> is <reading>かたな</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: This kanji is the same as the radical you learned, so it means <kanji>thousand</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic: Remember the thousand people going down the slide on a cross in the radical 千? Turns out each one of them was carrying a <kanji>thousand</kanji> <reading>cen</reading>ts (せん). Go ahead and try to calculate what a thousand times a thousand cents would come out to. It's quite a lot, actually. $10 (since 100 cents = 1 dollar).
extra_reading_mnemonic: 千葉 - There is only one place in Japan that has a thousand leaves and that's <kanji>Chiba</kanji>. Picture all of those leaves swirling around you on your vacation to Chiba. Beautiful. There's also a thousand <reading>chee</reading>se (ち) in Chiba, yum.

meaning_mnemonic:
<radical>Narwhal</radical> <radical>mouth</radical>s are on the <kanji>right</kanji> side of their head. In fact, some people didn't think they had mouths at all because they weren't looking from the right. Rookie mistake.

See how the "mouth" radical is to the right of the "narwhal" radical? That should help you remember that this means <kanji>right</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic: In their <kanji>right</kanji> hands, the narwhals shake hands with the <reading>you</reading>ths (ゆう). "To be on the right side of history, you must be kind for the younger generation," says the narwhal mouths.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Right</kanji> is <reading>みぎ</reading>.

右翼 (うよく) - Those in the <kanji>right</kanji> wing love eating <reading>u</reading>ni (う), not because they like the taste, but because uni is expensive. Fancy conservative right wingers..?

meaning_mnemonic: Imagine contorting yourself in such a way that your <radical>mouth</radical> now has your <radical>legs</radical> inside it. You've bent your body in all the wrong ways to achieve this. In fact, if you look at yourself, you look like a square now... You're just a person with <kanji>four</kanji> sides.
reading_mnemonic: Now that you have <kanji>four</kanji> sides, you look like a four-sided animal: the <reading>shee</reading>p (し). Look at yourself in the mirror and see an adorable four-sided sheep looking back at you. Imagine yourself with perfectly square wool. (You can only see four sides because mirrors aren't 3D. So you're a flat, cartoonish sheep.)
extra_reading_mnemonic:
You have to count to <kanji>four</kanji>. But you're tired. One... two... three... *<reading>YAWN</reading> (よん)* ... four. 

-<kanji>Four Things</kanji> is <reading>よっ</reading>つ. The ん part of よん gets converted to a small っ though, so watch out for that.

-<kanji>Fourth Day</kanji> is <reading>よっ</reading>か.

meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>dirt</radical> radical and the <kanji>dirt</kanji> kanji are the same!

(At first this looks like a cross in the ground, but it's actually something growing in the dirt. It's a little sprout, already rocking three leaves. And it's all thanks to that dirt! When you see this radical, think about how amazing it is that things just, like, grow in the dirt.)
reading_mnemonic: Who spends a lot of time in <kanji>dirt</kanji>? <reading>Do</reading>gs (ど) do! Dogs dig in dirt, they roll in dirt, sometimes they try to eat dirt (which isn't so great).
extra_reading_mnemonic:
If you walk barefoot outside, you'll have <kanji>dirt</kanji> on your <reading>toe</reading>s (と)! Those are dirty toes.

You look through the <kanji>dirt</kanji> or <kanji>soil</kanji> or <kanji>earth</kanji>. You're trying to find something. As you dig and sift, you come across not one but <reading>two chee</reading>ses (つち). Pull them out of the ground and put them in your mouth. They taste cheesy but a little dirty.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>evening</radical> radical and the <kanji>evening</kanji> kanji are the same. If you know the radical you know the meaning of the kanji.
reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>evening</kanji> is when all the <reading>you</reading>ths (ゆう) come outside to play.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical <radical>heaven</radical> is the same as the kanji <kanji>heaven</kanji>, making this an easy kanji to memorize.
reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Heaven</kanji>... nowadays, you need to do <reading>ten</reading> (てん) good things to get into heaven!
extra_reading_mnemonic: <reading>Ama</reading>nohashidate (天橋立) is a pine-covered sandbar that spans the mouth of Miyazu Bay in the scenic, coastal region of northern Kyoto Prefecture. Viewed from the mountains at either end of the bay, the Amanohashidate Sandbar (which roughly translates to "bridge in heaven") looks like a pathway between heaven and earth. The scene has been admired for centuries and is ranked among Japan's three most scenic views.

meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>child</radical> radical and the <kanji>child</kanji> kanji are exactly the same.

(Aww, see how they're wearing a cap and have their little arms stretched out? You can almost hear them saying "pick me up!" A very child-like child.)
reading_mnemonic:
The main reading here is し, so to remember it we'll use this mnemonic:

There is a <kanji>child</kanji> standing in front of you. You look closely at the child but something seems wrong. You rub your eyes and when you open them again, there is a <reading>shee</reading>p (し) in front of you. A sheep?! You yelp, blink again, and it's back to being a child. Are… are all children really just sheep?
extra_reading_mnemonic:
A <kanji>Child</kanji> is a <reading>こ</reading>.

椅子 (いす) - If a child falls off their chair, the parent will <reading>sue</reading> (す). Make sure your chairs are sturdy!

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>small</radical> radical and the <kanji>small</kanji> kanji are exactly the same.
reading_mnemonic: This <kanji>small</kanji> kanji would be the perfect gift to give to the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう). The Shougun loves little things, and the <kanji>little</kanji> kanji represents all of that.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Small</kanji> is <reading>ちいさい</reading>.

What are <kanji>small</kanji>? Kids (<reading>子</reading>) are small.

meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Narwhal</radical>s do <radical>construction</radical> with their <kanji>left</kanji> hands (or flippers, I guess). That's because all narwhals are left-handed!
reading_mnemonic: In their <kanji>left</kanji> hands, the narwhals all hold <reading>saw</reading>s (さ). That's because the ice for their homes is already there, so they just need to saw away at them to make the shapes they want. Narwhal construction is actually very simple.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Left</kanji> is <reading>ひだり</reading>. 

Imagine hearing someone to your <kanji>left</kanji> saying, "<reading>Hi Da'ri</reading>!" (ひだり) which is supposed to be "Hi There," or "Hi Dearie." You turn left and there's no one there. You hear it again, "Hi Da'ri!" Keep turning to the left until you find the person saying hi to you.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>hand</radical> radical and the <kanji>hand</kanji> kanji are identical in looks and meaning! That should make things easy!
reading_mnemonic: To remember the reading て we will use the word "television." You have great hands. Go ahead and look at them. OH MY GOD. You have little <reading>te</reading>levisions (て) on your hands. They are playing the funniest show you can think of, too, both hands at the same time.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
You open the trash <reading>chute</reading> (しゅ) with your hands. Throw away all these unnecessary televisions.

上手 (じょうず) - <kanji>Good At</kanji>. If you're good at your craft, you can get a trip paid to the <reading>zoo</reading> (ず).

下手 (へた) - <kanji>Unskillful</kanji>. If you're unskillful or bad at something and you complain about it, then you're just a <reading>hater</reading> (へた). Don't be a hater; get better.

meaning_mnemonic: On the <radical>ground</radical> you put <radical>barb</radical>s at the bottom of a <radical>slide</radical>. This is your special <kanji>talent</kanji>. When you go down the slide, you fly right past the barbs like some kind of daredevil. Any normal kid would land on the barbs and get hurt, but you have this talent.
reading_mnemonic:
But then people start to say that no human could have so much <kanji>talent</kanji>, that you must be a <reading>cy</reading>borg (さい). Are you really a talented cyborg?

Cyborgs have brain implants and cool bionic limbs, so they're basically the most talented people around.

meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for <radical>writing</radical> first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means <kanji>writing</kanji> as well.

(This looks like a stool with a lid on it, but it's actually a desk for writing. Do you see it? You can even see the pen sticking up in the middle. Think of all the beautiful writing that's been produced here. Letters, novels, essays — any kind of writing you can think of.)
reading_mnemonic: You always put <kanji>writing</kanji> on your <reading>bun</reading>s (ぶん) to keep them from getting eaten by the bun <reading>mon</reading>ster (もん). What kind of writing? Usually it's just an X to show the monster these buns are off-limits. (In fact, it kind of looks like the X part in 文. Hmm…)

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> radical and <kanji>sun</kanji> kanji are the same, huzzah! Also, if you want to remember <kanji>day</kanji> as well, you can just think about how a day is the time it takes for the sun to cross the sky.
reading_mnemonic:
There are so many on'yomi for this kanji, but since this kanji is so important and common, you'll end up learning them all eventually whether you want to or not. For now, you're only going to have to learn one of the readings, and that one is にち.

The <kanji>sun</kanji> is so hot. It focused its rays to take out one man... and that man is Friedrich <reading>Nietzsche</reading> (にち), famous philosopher. He philosophized one too many things about the sun, so the sun decided it was time he paid.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
The truth (実) is that you don't know if the <kanji>sun</kanji> will rise tomorrow. But then you see two suns? Are we on Earth still?! Is this a dream?! <reading>Gee! Two</reading> (じつ) suns! 

What do you feel from the <kanji>sun</kanji>? You feel the <reading>he</reading>at (ひ).

For <kanji>day counters</kanji>, we have 日 as <reading>か</reading>. For example, Fifth Day 五日 = いつ<reading>か</reading>.

For <kanji>days of the week</kanji>, we have 日 as <reading>び</reading>. For example, Friday 金曜日 = きんよう<reading>び</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>moon</kanji> kanji is made up of the <radical>moon</radical> radical. This kanji is also used to mean <kanji>month</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>moon</kanji> really <reading>gets</reading> (げつ) to your <reading>guts</reading> (がつ). Staring at the moon for too long warms your guts. Not like a werewolf, warm-non-wolf?
extra_reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Moon</kanji> is <reading>つき</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: This is another kanji that is the same as the radical. Both <radical>tree</radical> and <kanji>tree</kanji> are the same in looks and meaning.
reading_mnemonic: You’re walking through the trees, looking at them. Suddenly, you trip and fall. The <kanji>tree</kanji>s start to <reading>mock</reading> (もく) you. They're tall and you're short, no fair! But at least I have legs and can move around!
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Tree</kanji> is <reading>き</reading>. 

You walk up to the <kanji>tree</kanji>. You take out your <reading>key</reading> (き) and put it in the slot, opening the door in the tree so you can slip inside. Your secret key to open the tree house!

meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for <radical>book</radical> first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means <kanji>book</kanji> as well.

(What's something useful you can get out of a tree? A book! Just cut that book right out of the tree trunk. If you think about it, every tree contains unlimited book potential. It's just a shame they have to be cut down to make the books…)

Take note that the second, third, and fourth meanings of this kanji are <kanji>origin</kanji>, <kanji>real</kanji>, and <kanji>main</kanji>. You can figure this out by thinking about how books mainly have their origins in real life.
reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Book</kanji>s are one of the best ways to <reading>hone</reading> (ほん) your intellect, you know?
extra_reading_mnemonic: 熊本県 (くま<reading>もと</reading>けん) is <kanji>Kumamoto Prefecture</kanji>.

meaning_mnemonic: There is a line on the <radical>ground</radical> so you <radical>stop</radical>, making a giant sign pop up that says <kanji>CORRECT</kanji>! You obeyed the rules of the road and did the correct thing. Good on you.
reading_mnemonic: You did the <kanji>correct</kanji> thing, so here's your reward: a <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい) from the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう) himself!
extra_reading_mnemonic: 正しい (ただしい) - After you get the answer <kanji>correct</kanji> a clown jumps out of nowhere yelling "<reading>Ta-da</reading> (ただ)!!!" WHOA, that was scary. You almost slashed the clown with your new saber but luckily the Shougun says, "its ok he's safe".

visually_similar_kanji: 泳, 球, 永, 氷, 求
meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>water</radical> radical and the <kanji>water</kanji> kanji are the same.
reading_mnemonic:
Imagine a lake (i.e. a whole bunch of <kanji>water</kanji>). On a tree there is an awesome tire <reading>swi</reading>ng (すい). You get onto the tire swing and you are swinging back and forth. The water is right in front of you, and you are able to use the swing to throw yourself into the water. 

It’s a lot colder than you expected, and you come back to the surface, gasping for breath. The water gets into your mouth and you taste it. How strange, it’s very, very <reading>swee</reading>t. Imagine the sweetness of the water and how weird it is (really really sweet, this water is).
extra_reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Water</kanji> is <reading>みず</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>fire</radical> radical and the <kanji>fire</kanji> kanji are the same as each other.
reading_mnemonic:
Whenever we need to remember か, we use the word <reading>car</reading>.

You see <kanji>fire</kanji>. What's on fire? It's someone's <reading>car</reading> (か)! Oh no, it's like a movie! Get away before it explodes!
extra_reading_mnemonic:
What comes off of <kanji>fire</kanji>? Lots and lots of <reading>hea</reading>t (ひ). Feel it coming off the fire, touching and warming your face.

火照る (<reading>ほ</reading>てる) - When are you going <kanji>to feel hot</kanji>? When is your face going <kanji>to flush</kanji>? When you see your <reading>hoe</reading> (garden tool hoe, I mean).

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>dog</radical> radical and <kanji>dog</kanji> kanji are exactly the same!
reading_mnemonic:
A <kanji>Dog</kanji> is a <reading>いぬ</reading>.

Every <kanji>dog</kanji> likes to <reading>ea</reading>t <reading>noo</reading>dles (いぬ). Like that movie where the dogs share a noodle and end up kissing, right? So when you see 犬, just imagine how those two eat noodles.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 猟犬 (りょうけん) - Who has the best (hunting <kanji>dog</kanji>) in the world? <reading>Ken</reading> (けん) from Street Fighter! His dog is also named Ken, because that's how Ken and Ken do things.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>king</radical> has a big <radical>drop</radical> of liquid in his hand... but then he bounces it! The drop was really a <kanji>ball</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Ball</kanji> is <reading>たま</reading> / Tama.

~~~ When he's done playing with it, the king gives his <kanji>ball</kanji> to <reading>Tama</reading>ra (たま), the resident ball girl, for safekeeping.

visually_similar_kanji: 主, 往, 注, 住, 柱
meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>king</radical> radical and the <kanji>king</kanji> kanji are the same!
reading_mnemonic: When you see the <kanji>king</kanji> you need to say, "<reading>Oh</reading> (おう) King! Oh King, oh no, oh why are you looking at me like that? Oh King... you aren't going to chop off my head are you? OH NO!"

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>rice paddy</radical> radical and the <kanji>rice paddy</kanji> kanji are the same, making this one super easy to remember, at least meaning-wise.
reading_mnemonic:
To remember the reading た, we use the word "taco."

You're in the <kanji>rice field</kanji>... but when you lean down to examine the rice more closely, you see that it's not rice that's growing, it's a bunch of little <reading>ta</reading>cos (た), blossoming out of the ground.
extra_reading_mnemonic: You take a bite out of the <kanji>rice paddy</kanji> taco and even smush some tacos together, both actions create a <reading>den</reading>t (でん) in the tacos.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical <radical>white</radical> and the kanji <kanji>white</kanji> are the same.
reading_mnemonic:
The <kanji>white</kanji> team was the first to be able to <reading>hack</reading> (はく) the <kanji>white</kanji> iPhone.

Imagine two teams (black and white), wearing their team colors, working really hard on hacking the iPhone. It is a huge contest, and people are watching with a lot of tension, to see who will hack the white iPhone first. Feel that tension, and see the colors separating them so vividly. The colors are important, and the excitement of the winner holding up the hacked iPhone is too.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>White</kanji> surrounds you. The <reading>sheer</reading> (<reading>しろ</reading>) amount of white is overwhelming. Blinding white light, close your eyes and wait until it's over. It won't be long.

Sometimes it's <reading>しら</reading> like with 白菊 (しらぎく) White Chrysanthemum. Watch out for the rendaku on きく.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>eye</radical> radical and <kanji>eye</kanji> kanji are the same as each other, so now you know them both.
reading_mnemonic: Your <kanji>eyes</kanji> are your <reading>め</reading>.
extra_reading_mnemonic: Mean people slant their <kanji>eye</kanji>s as a way to <reading>mock</reading> (もく) you. What?! So mean! Why would they do that?!

meaning_mnemonic: The radical <radical>stand</radical> and the kanji <kanji>stand</kanji> are the same thing, so now you know them both.
reading_mnemonic: Think of someone who has to <kanji>stand</kanji> up straight for you. These people are pros in hospitality. These are the doormen at the <reading>Ritz</reading> (りつ).
extra_reading_mnemonic:
You have <kanji>to stand</kanji> up in order to wave goodbye to someone. When you stand up, you also say <reading>ta</reading>-ta (た)!

立つ (<kanji>To Stand</kanji>) vs. 立てる(<kanji>To Stand Something Up</kanji>)

meaning_mnemonic: You cut the <radical>leaf</radical> with your <radical>sword</radical> into <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> pieces!
reading_mnemonic: Now that you have <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> pieces of tiny leaf paper, you decide to turn them into a <reading>man</reading>ga (まん)! Each little leaf piece will become a panel.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 万人 (ばんにん) - If we're talking about ten thousand persons, then we might as well be talking about all people and everybody, because that's a lot of people, you know? <kanji>All people</kanji> will <reading>ban</reading> your manga if it sucks. Make sure it's good!

meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for <radical>now</radical> first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means <kanji>now</kanji> as well.

(It's a bit tough to see, but it kind of looks like a fancy clock. The 𠆢 is the top part hanging over the clock. The ラ shows a triangular clock face with a little cuckoo on top, peeking out to tell you this means now — right now!)
reading_mnemonic: Right <kanji>now</kanji> the <reading>con</reading>dors (こん) are here. In this very moment, take a look and appreciate this very large bird of the Vulture family.
extra_reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Now</kanji> is <reading>いま</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>head</radical> has a <radical>person</radical> <kanji>inside</kanji> it!
reading_mnemonic:
You know this kanji means <kanji>inside</kanji>, so you can keep thinking about the person that's inside you, running around. You finally discover him, and try to take him out, but before you can, he pulls out a <reading>kni</reading>fe (ない) and threatens to cut you if you do anything irrational. You pull our your own knife. 

A knife fight?! Inside?! It's a battle between yourself!
extra_reading_mnemonic: You were looking <kanji>inside</kanji> and you wanna get to what's within. Look inside. <reading>Ooh, cheese</reading> (うち)! Your favorite. That's what you really want, you cheesey dream.

meaning_mnemonic: You’ve got a <radical>winter</radical> with lots of <radical>ice</radical>. But doesn't any winter have lots of ice? Exactly. That's why this is just <kanji>winter</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Winter</kanji> is also the time of year you give out presents: "One fu' you, one fu' you and… one <reading>fu' you</reading> (ふゆ)!"
extra_reading_mnemonic: 春夏秋冬 (shunkashuutou / しゅんかしゅうとう) - <kanji>Winter</kanji> in <reading>とう</reading>きょう sounds pretty nice. Apparently that also is an Indonesian movie from 2016, but I haven't watched it.

other_meanings: Minute, Divide, Portion, Separate, Understand, Sort, Split, Classify, Share
meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>fins</radical> that fell onto my <radical>sword</radical> were sliced into many <kanji>part</kanji>s. Following this logic, this also means <kanji>minute</kanji>, which is part of an hour, and <kanji>divide</kanji>, which is the action of splitting something into many parts.
reading_mnemonic:
Now that the fins have been cut into neat <kanji>part</kanji>s, it's time to cut something else: <reading>bun</reading>s (ぶん).

This is how you feed your people: neatly divided, delicious buns. Picture these delicious buns divided into perfectly shaped parts. Yummy.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
How many <kanji>minute</kanji>s of <reading>fun</reading> (ふん) will you have today? Lots and lots of minutes, I hope!

分かる (わかる) - This word means to understand, which might surprise you if you remember that the kanji 分 means part. Think of it this way: to understand something you have to break it down into its parts to see how it works. Whenever you try <kanji>to understand</kanji> something, you just start screaming "<reading>WAAAAAAAAAHHHH</reading>" (わ). It helps you focus and concentrate on what you’re trying to understand, to the dismay of everyone around you. WAAAAAAAAAHHHH.

分かる (<kanji>To Understand</kanji>) vs. 分ける (<kanji>To Divide Something</kanji>).

meaning_mnemonic: If you have <radical>seven</radical> <radical>swords</radical>, there's only so much you can do with them. The main thing? Probably using them to <kanji>cut</kanji> something.
reading_mnemonic: Because having seven swords for yourself is too much, you decide to take the swords and divide them up amongst pairs of people. You <kanji>cut</kanji> them into pairs, and give <reading>sets</reading> (せつ) to everyone who needs them in the village.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
When you think <reading>to cut</reading> something, what do you think about cutting? One thing is cutting down a tree, which is also known as <reading>木</reading> (き). You 切る a 木.

切る (<kanji>To Cut</kanji>) vs. 切れる (<kanji>To Be Cut</kanji>)

meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji is the same as the radical — it means <kanji>north</kanji>.

(You only have some ice and a stick for your spoon, because you're way up north. At the top of the world, there's only ice to eat, and — if you're lucky — a bit of stick for flavor. That's the north for you.)
reading_mnemonic: You go north, and notice that everyone has a keytar (きた). You know, those keyboards that people hold and play like a guitar? You came to the north side! きた!
extra_reading_mnemonic: 東北 (とうほく) - The East North area of Japan is called (Tohoku), or the Tohoku region. In Tohoku there's a lot of <reading>hocu</reading>s (ほく) pocus going on. Basically, if you're in Japan's northeast, watch out… A lot of mountain hermits live up in those parts, practicing their weird hocus pocus. Don't let 'em getcha.

visually_similar_kanji: 年, 矢, 失, 朱, 件, 牛, 生
meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>slide</radical> is <radical>dry</radical> at <kanji>noon</kanji>. The sun is brightest at noon, so it dries the morning dew off the slide, making noon the perfect time to slide.
reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Noon</kanji> also happens to be the time <reading>Go</reading>dzilla (ご) decided to attack. He likes to attack dry slides, for some reason.

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>triceratops</radical> is lying out to <radical>dry</radical>. But it's so big, and it's lying on its side, so only <kanji>half</kanji> of it gets dry.
reading_mnemonic: "You're half wet and half dry! I will cut you in <kanji>half</kanji> with my laser blaster so you're proper again," a voice says. It is  <reading>Han</reading> Solo (はん), the anti-establishment guy who hates when things aren't even.

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>narwhal</radical> sitting on a <radical>stool</radical> is your <kanji>friend</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic: "Hi <kanji>friend</kanji>," says the narwhal. "We are in our <reading>you</reading>ths." (ゆう).
extra_reading_mnemonic: "We should make as many <kanji>friend</kanji>s as we can while we are young. We need more <reading>とも</reading>だち! More 友達!" You agree with the narhwal sitting on a stool.

meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for <radical>old</radical> first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means <kanji>old</kanji> as well.

(Put a cross over the mouth of a container full of all the old things you no longer need. They've all served their purpose but have gotten old, so it's now time to let them rest in peace under the cross. Goodbye, old things!)

Note: This "old" does not refer to people. Think of it as "old things" instead.
reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Old</kanji> things are misunderstood by the <reading>子</reading>s (こ) of the world.

*Note:* Come up with a 子 character you can use for all the こ reading mnemonics going forward. This child will show up many times throughout your mnemonic journey, and it will help if you imagine the same character the whole time.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
古い (ふるい) - If you're <kanji>old</kanji>, you're also <reading>full</reading> (ふる) of memories. And you're probably full of old secrets. And you're full from old people food.

*** This word is used for things like clothes, food and friendships, but not for people! So a 古い友人 (old friend) is someone you've been friends with for a long time, not an elderly friend.

other_meanings: Big Machine, Big Device, Device, Stand
meaning_mnemonic: You have a <radical>private</radical> <radical>mouth</radical> that's a <kanji>machine</kanji>. But you have to keep your machine mouth private because it would scare all the non-machine people around you.
reading_mnemonic:
To make sure they can't tell what's <kanji>machine</kanji> and what's human, you <reading>dye</reading> (だい) the mouth to make it look like skin. You find dye the same shade as your normal mouth and just slap it on there.

Kissing <kanji>machine</kanji> is seen as weird, so people <reading>tie</reading> you up for that act. You think people are so close-minded, when will this discrimination against machine-kind end?! But maybe they have a point?

meaning_mnemonic: You're known to get the ailment <radical>evening</radical> <radical>toe</radical>, which is when your toe catches on fire after getting really, really hot (imagine this happening, ouch!). The only way to fix it is to cool your toe down, and the best way to do that is to go <kanji>outside</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic: You go <kanji>outside</kanji> (you’re not supposed to be out there at night!) and you’re accosted by a couple of guys. Then, all of a sudden, <reading>Guy</reading> (がい) Fawkes jumps from the roof above you and takes them out, then starts running. “Guy Fawkes!” you yell after him!
extra_reading_mnemonic:
<kanji>Outside</kanji> is <reading>そと</reading>.

外す (はずす) - The kanji 外 means outside, and the meaning of this verb is somewhat related. It means to remove something. Think of it like this — if you remove your watch, you are putting it "outside" of its usual spot (your wrist), right? If you're going <kanji>to remove</kanji>  something from its usual spot, you'd better put on your <reading>haz</reading>mat (はず) suit. 広げる (<kanji>To Spread Something</kanji>) vs. 広がる (<kanji>To Spread Out</kanji>).

extra_reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Heart</kanji> is <reading>こころ</reading>!

meaning_mnemonic: The radical and the kanji for <kanji>door</kanji> are the same!

The radical and the kanji for <kanji>direction</kanji> are the same! Huzzah!

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>bright</radical> radical and the <kanji>bright</kanji> kanji are the same!

extra_reading_mnemonic:

What's a <kanji>bright</kanji> color? <reading>赤</reading> (あか), aka "red," obviously. Think of a really bright あか color when you see 明るい.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>stop</radical> radical is the same as the <kanji>stop</kanji> kanji.

止める (<reading>と</reading>める or <reading>や</reading>める) (<kanji>To Stop Something</kanji>).

止まる (<reading>と</reading>まる) (<kanji>To Stop</kanji>).

meaning_mnemonic: Someone breaks part of your <radical>window</radical>. Who did this? It was your <kanji>mother</kanji>!

There's just too much <kanji>hair</kanji>!

extra_reading_mnemonic: Look down! You're holding something covered in <kanji>fur</kanji>. It's a furry <reading>ke</reading>ttle (け)! It's the weirdest kettle you've ever seen, but presumably it keeps the water hot for much longer. It might help with mowing the fur too.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical and the kanji for <kanji>father</kanji> are the same.

<kanji>Father</kanji>s love <reading>ちち</reading>s. Is your father Goku?!

After eating <kanji>raw</kanji> fish, my yoga teacher and I say <reading>nama</reading>ste (なま) to the sushi chef, bowing low to show our appreciation.

写す (<kanji>To Copy</kanji>) vs. 写る (<kanji>To Be In A Photograph</kanji>).

Imagine yourself going to that place to see the “night mouth.”), and appears only one month out of the year (more on this in a second). The “evening mouth” is the most famous thing in the _____ area (this is the area you choose). He’s so <kanji>famous</kanji> that everybody knows his <kanji>name</kanji> (“Evening Mouth.”).

kunyomi: あたら, あら, にい
visually_similar_kanji: 規, 親, 視, 折, 祈, 析, 斬
meaning_mnemonic: You <radical>stand</radical> on top of a <radical>tree</radical> with an <radical>axe</radical>. You're going to cut down this tree to let a <kanji>new</kanji> tree grow.
reading_mnemonic: You cut down the tree to make room for a <kanji>new</kanji> one, but it falls on your <reading>shin</reading> (しん).
extra_reading_mnemonic:
新しい (あたらしい) - As a reward/apology for your job (ouch your shin), your family buys you a <kanji>new</kanji> Atari! You're so excited! But wait... what's this? This is no Atari. This is an <reading>Atara</reading>... a knockoff video game system :( At least it'll still be fun to play.

新た (あらた) - Your parents also gave you a <kanji>newly</kanji> wrapped present. You rip it open to find they got you <reading>a raw</reading> (あら) steak. Getting a new steak is cool and all, but a raw steak is pretty gross. It's dripping blood all over the place. Gotta cook it up for some yummy steak.

meaning_mnemonic: Take the <radical>moon</radical> <radical>stamp</radical> on the <radical>stool</radical> in front of you and use it on all of your <kanji>clothes</kanji>. Now even if you sell or lose a piece of <kanji>clothing</kanji>, you'll be able to find it again by checking for your special moon stamp.
reading_mnemonic: A few days later you're with a friend when you recognize the <kanji>clothes</kanji> they're wearing. You grab it, rip it off, and scream, "<reading>F**k</reading> (ふく) you!" There is your moon stamp! These are your clothes, so your friend must have stolen them from you!!

meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>compare</radical> radical and the <kanji>compare</kanji> kanji are exactly the same! Huzzah!

It looks like two slightly different versions of the spoon radical. Look closely at these two spoons. <kanji>Compare</kanji> their differences.
reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Compare</kanji> the <reading>he</reading>at (ひ) today with the heat yesterday. Is it hotter today? It's up to you to compare.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 比べる (くらべる) - To prepare for the heat, let's look at this <reading>cooler</reading> (くら). Now look at this other cooler. We need <kanji>to compare</kanji> the two coolers. Think about all the features each one has and really compare, like you have a list or something.

visually_similar_kanji: 水, 氷, 永, 詠
meaning_mnemonic: If a <radical>tsunami</radical> is going to last an <radical>eternity</radical> you better learn how to <kanji>swim</kanji> now. We'll be under water for the rest of time and if you can't swim you're not gonna make it.
reading_mnemonic: <reading>Oy</reading> (およ)! Oy, stop daydreaming about <kanji>swim</kanji>ming and actually do it!
extra_reading_mnemonic:
水泳 (すいえい) - You <kanji>swim</kanji> to find some <reading>a</reading>corns (えい). The motivation to swim is from the hope to plant some trees for land.

Note that 水泳 will usually refer to swimming as a sport or organized activity. When talking about swimming as a general action, 泳ぎ and 泳ぐ are more commonly used.

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>cow</radical> with <radical>wing</radical>s is flying in the air. What a strange <kanji>thing</kanji>! You've heard of flying pigs before, but cows? This is a new and strange thing indeed! Cows with wings! What a silly thing.
reading_mnemonic: You want a <kanji>thing</kanji> to help you fly with the cow so you put on your flying <reading>boots</reading> (ぶつ). Your flying boots are a pretty strange thing in themselves, but they're the only way you can keep up.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
What game has the most <kanji>thing</kanji>s in it? <reading>Mono</reading>poly (もの). You can choose from a bunch of random things to play as, you know? And no one actually knows what those things are. What's a thimble anyway? Just call it a thing.

荷物 (にもつ) - All their luggage just got thrown into various <reading>moats</reading> (もつ) along the countryside. It's going to take them forever to collect their luggage from these moats and by then it'll be all soggy. Dangit...

meaning_mnemonic:
Every <radical>rice paddy</radical> sits <radical>jammed in</radical> to the <kanji>world</kanji>.

The world is basically just a bunch of rice paddies smooshed together, if you think about it.
reading_mnemonic:
To get around this <kanji>world</kanji> of rice paddies, you need to use a <reading>kay</reading>ak (かい).

A rice paddy is mostly made up of water, just like our world, and you don't want to have wet feet. Use the power of your kayak to become a world traveler.

meaning_mnemonic: Go to the <radical>tent</radical> and take the <radical>lantern</radical> from it, then we will be ready for <kanji>departure</kanji>. We can't leave the lantern inside of the tent; that's a fire hazard. We'd best take it with us before the departure. Don't you agree?
reading_mnemonic: Oh! Don't forget your <reading>hats</reading> (はつ) either. Wouldn’t want to start a <kanji>departure</kanji> without hats or a lantern. That'd be a cold journey.

visually_similar_kanji: 阻, 租, 粗, 祖, 狙, 組
meaning_mnemonic: You need to look a <radical>tree</radical> in the <radical>eye</radical> to gain a <kanji>mutual</kanji> respect for each other. Stand up straight, look the tree directly in its eye(s). If it looks right back, you know things are mutual.
reading_mnemonic: If your respect for the tree is <kanji>mutual</kanji> with the respect the tree feels for you, you'll be able to see the tree's <reading>sou</reading>l (そう). Right now its soul looks pretty sad, like it's trying to say, "Why are your people cutting down all my friends? I thought we had a mutual understanding."
extra_reading_mnemonic:
相手 (あいて) (Now, what do you think your mutual doer might be? It’s someone who shares the same activities or tasks with you. This person could be your <kanji>partner</kanji>, <kanji>companion</kanji>, or even an <kanji>opponent</kanji> in certain situations.) - Your (tree with eyes?) partner wouldn't be your partner without you. Your partner is: <reading>I</reading> (あい) and you. Remember that as you gaze into your partner's <reading>eye</reading>s. "I and you."

首相 (しゅしょう) (The neck minister? This meaning prime minister makes sense if you think about the neck being the most important part of the body, kind of like the head!) - The first <kanji>prime minister</kanji>s of Japan were actually the <reading>sho</reading>guns (しょう)… kind of.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>eye</radical> of a <radical>lion</radical>, still <radical>small</radical> and curious, gazes upon the <kanji>prefecture</kanji> that will one day become his. He's a small lion, but once he grows up, everything reflected in his eye will be his prefecture to rule over.
reading_mnemonic: This small lion's <kanji>prefecture</kanji> is being protected by <reading>Ken</reading> (けん) the samurai, because the lion is too small to protect all of this land himself. Ken the samurai is used to wandering far and wide, so one prefecture is nothing to him.

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>horns</radical>-having <radical>king</radical> that's <radical>big</radical> is a true <kanji>beauty</kanji>. Big is <kanji>beautiful</kanji>, and that's all the more true for kings and the kings' horns.
reading_mnemonic:
The big horns-having king's <kanji>beauty</kanji> has attracted a swarm of <reading>bee</reading>s (び). The horns are so beautiful that the bees have mistaken it for a flower.

The bees are swarming around the big horns and the horns-having king, marvelling at its beauty and trying to figure out how to get nectar from it.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
美しい - You look at someone who is <kanji>beautiful</kanji> (like the horns-having big king). What an easy life they've lived. No hard work and all they do is pamper themselves to stay beautiful. Feel disgusted. You walk up to this person and say: "<reading>U too cushy</reading>! (うつくしい).

Sorry for adding the whole word in there for the reading mnemonic, but I thought it worked out better that way. Just know that the word isn't うつくしいしい or something weird like that. The hiragana on the end is part of the mnemonic as well.

visually_similar_kanji: 古, 草, 岩, 若, 著
meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>flowers</radical> have grown <radical>old</radical>, so they're <kanji>suffering</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic: If a flower or a person is growing old and <kanji>suffering</kanji>, give them a <reading>coo</reading>kie (く). No one can resist a good cookie. It will ease your suffering, or at least distract you for a little bit.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
苦しい (くるしい) - Everything is really <kanji>painful</kanji> right now. Why? You have something heavy on top of you, <reading>cru</reading>shing (くる) you.

苦い (にがい) - The taste is so <kanji>bitter tasting</kanji> that you fall to your knees really, really hard. Luckily, you were wearing your <reading>knee gua</reading>rds (にが). Feel the relief that you were wearing them. Ack, no relief now. It's still bitter in your mouth.

The kanji for 苦 means suffering. And eating bitter tasting things will cause you to suffer.

visually_similar_kanji: 衣, 裏, 俵, 麦
meaning_mnemonic: Sometimes <radical>life</radical> (with no slide) gives you a <radical>kick</radical>, and you have to <kanji>express</kanji> yourself to deal with it! How do you express yourself? On the <kanji>surface</kanji> (of your face)!
reading_mnemonic:
You need to <kanji>express</kanji> yourself, so you call up a friend and say "<reading>Heyo</reading>!" (ひょう).

Imagine yourself saying it more like ひょう, though. ひょう man!
extra_reading_mnemonic:
表す (あらわす) - You're struggling <kanji>to express something</kanji> to your friends: namely, that you <reading>are a wa</reading>lrus (あらわ). All your friends think you're a human, so they'll be shocked when you express to them the fact that, actually, you are a walrus. You need to get it off your chest though… Your big, blubbery walrus chest.

You schedule to meet with your friend to talk who just gave you coordinates ofthe meetup location. So you're standing there, staring at <kanji>the front</kanji> of this building. You spend some time gazing at it before you realize what it is. "<reading>Oh</reading>, <reading>mote</reading>l (おもて)," you say aloud. <kanji>The surface</kanji> of this building really gave it away. "Oh, motel!"

表 refers to the visible, outward-facing side of something, in contrast to the hidden, back side. It's used for surfaces on display, like the front of a building, the face of a coin, the cover of a book, or the top surface of a package.

meaning_mnemonic: When a <radical>helicopter</radical> is piloted by a <radical>woman</radical>, it stirs an insatiable <kanji>need</kanji> in her. She doesn't know what it is. But she needs it. And that's why she's flying around looking for it!
reading_mnemonic: Finally she knows what she <kanji>need</kanji>s! It's <reading>yo</reading>gurt (よう)! Delicious, creamy yogurt! All this piloting sure makes a woman hungry for some yogurt.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 要る (いる) - She is going <kanji>to need</kanji> an <reading>ea</reading>gle. The helicopter woman needs a companion (and backup) when flying up in the sky. (Good thing they both like yogurt.)

meaning_mnemonic: If you want to <radical>say</radical> something at a <radical>ceremony</radical> for <radical>construction</radical> workers you're going to have to <kanji>try</kanji> really hard. Construction is loud, so if you want to be heard you have to <kanji>attempt</kanji> to be louder than the drilling and smashing and digging and handing out of awards.
reading_mnemonic: You <kanji>try</kanji> to get their attention the only way you know how, by lifting a <reading>shee</reading>p (し) above your head. The sheep baas and suddenly everything is silent, all eyes are on you. Well, they're on the sheep.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
試す (ためす) - We have this wild animal. I want you <kanji>to attempt</kanji> to <reading>tame</reading> (ため) it. Now, imagine trying to tame this wild animal. Yeehaw!

試みる (こころみる) - You know how when you <kanji>try to do something</kanji> you put your whole heart into it? Well, think of that in Japanese. You put your whole <reading>心</reading> (こころ) into it.

meaning_mnemonic: You  <radical>say</radical> things around a  <radical>fire</radical>. In fact there are two  <radical>fire</radical>s, and you're <kanji>talk</kanji>ing with a group of people, all sitting around two nice campfires.
reading_mnemonic: You <kanji>talk</kanji> in this intense, fiery way all the way until <reading>dawn</reading> (だん), but no longer! Once dawn comes the discussion needs to be concluded.

visually_similar_kanji: 貝, 魚, 具, 急, 頁
meaning_mnemonic: When you're in <radical>prison</radical>, whoever ends up with the <radical>shellfish</radical> will <kanji>lose</kanji>. It's the game all prisoners play. It's like keep away from the shellfish. And if you end up with the shellfish BZZZZTT that's it, you're the loser.
reading_mnemonic: If you <kanji>lose</kanji>, you're a <reading>foo</reading>l (ふ). All you had to do was not hold the prison shellfish. It really shouldn't have been that hard to not lose, ya fool.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 負ける - You <kanji>lose</kanji> your tournament/soccer game/whatever (you decide something applicable to you). You're sad about this. Who's there to comfort you? Your <reading>Ma</reading> (ま). She's a nice lady.

meaning_mnemonic:
(Different radicals: Put a LID on your YEN and things can get spicy. It's spicy because it can be hard when you have a limit on your money.)

The <radical>spicy</radical> radical and <kanji>spicy</kanji> kanji are exactly the same! Hot!
reading_mnemonic: When you eat <kanji>spicy</kanji> food, it gives a <reading>から</reading>て chop to your mouth. That's where that spicy feeling comes from!
extra_reading_mnemonic:
辛い - Depending on the context, the reading for this word could be からい or つらい.

The つらい reading is the <kanji>difficult</kanji> or <kanji>painful</kanji> one. You can remember this because <reading>two Ra</reading>s (つら) are way more difficult to deal with than one Ra.

visually_similar_kanji: 版, 仮, 阪, 板, 坂, 飯, 販
meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>scooter</radical> is <radical>anti</radical> scoot. It doesn't want to run. So you have to <kanji>return</kanji> it.
reading_mnemonic: You <kanji>return</kanji> to the store and wait in line to return the scooter but the person working returns doesn't want you to return it. He stares you dead in the eyes, and tries to negotiate. "If you don't return the scooter, I'll give you this <reading>hen</reading> (へん)!"
extra_reading_mnemonic:
You also have <kanji>to return</kanji> the <reading>Ca</reading>r <reading>e</reading>gg (かえ) you found on the side of the road. It will birth a little car, but it needs its mother. So, you try to figure out how to return this weird car egg.

返る (<kanji>To Be Returned</kanji>) vs. 返す (<kanji>To Return Something</kanji> - This is more like "to return a thing" rather than returning home, which would be 帰る)

meaning_mnemonic: On its <radical>scooter</radical>, a creature with <radical>horns</radical> from <radical>heaven</radical> will take things you want to <kanji>send</kanji> there.
reading_mnemonic: You want to <kanji>send</kanji> your <reading>sou</reading>l (そう) to heaven. I mean, you don't want it to go to some of those other places you've heard of, so why not send your soul?
extra_reading_mnemonic:
送る (おくる) - You need <kanji>to send</kanji> an entire <reading>oak</reading> (おく) tree in the mail, but it's too big. Imagine yourself dragging one to the post office. They tell you that you can't send that here... Go to the oak sending facilities. 

Maybe this creature with horns from heaven with a scooter can help you send this oak tree?

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>clown</radical> <radical>building</radical> is over in that <kanji>part</kanji> of town. We keep the clown part as separate as we can from the rest of the normal people. In fact, the entire clown education <kanji>department</kanji> and their clown <kanji>club</kanji>s have to stay in their part, they can't come in ours.
reading_mnemonic: You see, that <kanji>part</kanji> of town is full of <reading>boo</reading>ze (ぶ). Clowns need a lot of booze to keep their charade going, so we just let them have it. But they aren't allowed in our part anymore, because they all stink of nasty clown booze.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
部屋 (へや) (If you have a part of a roof, that part is your room.) - Imagine you're renting out a <kanji>room</kanji>, but all you hear at night is a constant "<reading>heh</reading> (へ)… heh... heh... hehehe". An incessant snickering, coming from somewhere inside your room. Hehehe. Maybe this place is a clown building, and a clown with booze is still there?

部屋 is a bit tricky because it's one of the few Japanese words that use the へ reading for 部. You'll just have to remember this one is special.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>heavy</radical> radical and the <kanji>heavy</kanji> kanji are the same.
reading_mnemonic: In your hand is a very <kanji>heavy</kanji> <reading>jew</reading>el (じゅう). Real jewels are always heavier than they look.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
重い (おもい) - You're lifting something that's really <kanji>heavy</kanji> (like the jewel). Oof! You lift it above your head. You're so awesome. You scream: "<reading>OH! MO</reading>RE!" (おも) they put more. You yell it again: "OH, MORE!" and again: "OH, MORE!" Go ahead and act this out wherever you are, pretending like you're holding a couch or two or three over your head, saying "OH MORE!"

All the things you've <kanji>stack</kanji>ed up were in preparation for your new <reading>casa</reading> (かさ). With everything inside boxes and neatly piled up, you're finally ready to move into your new casa. Hooray!

重なる (<kanji>To Be Piled Up</kanji>) vs. 重ねる (<kanji>To Stack</kanji> or <kanji>To Pile Up</kanji>).

貴重 (きちょう) - Keep things <kanji>precious</kanji> to you very close, because the evil Mrs. <reading>Chou</reading> (ちょう) will come and steal them away if you don't. She'll take all the <kanji>valuable</kanji> things you have and destroy them.

貴重 is used especially when something is rare, important, or hard to replace. You can use it for physical things, but you'll see it used to show appreciation for intangible things too, like 貴重なご意見 (your valuable opinion) or 貴重な体験 (a precious experience).

meaning_mnemonic:
A <radical>horse</radical> and a <radical>squid</radical> are going to <kanji>test</kanji> you.

Imagine the horse and squid in a big testing room, getting ready to test you. What are they testing you on? Weirdly, they're going to test you on all the kanji that use horse and squid radicals. You ready?
reading_mnemonic:
The <kanji>test</kanji> is being supervised by <reading>Ken</reading> (けん) the samurai.

To make sure you don't cheat on the horse and the squid test, Ken the samurai is watching you closely, pacing up and down. Every now and then, he waves his katana menacingly.

meaning_mnemonic: There is a famous fishing lure inventor, working on his best work ever. He’s old, and he’s been trying to make the best fishing lure for the last 50 years, and knows this will be his last invention. Then he figures it out. He takes one <radical>barb</radical>, and connects the end of it to the top of another <radical>barb</radical>. When he does this, he knows his work is finally <kanji>finish</kanji>ed.
reading_mnemonic: How does the fish lure maker test his newly <kanji>finish</kanji>ed lure out? The one he just finished? He gets in a <reading>row</reading> (りょう) boat and rows out into the sea.

meaning_mnemonic: You have <radical>fins</radical> in <radical>private</radical>. But, you want the world to see them, so you take them <kanji>public</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic: You head out into the <kanji>public</kanji> where everyone can see your fins, but... things have changed. All people are the same. There are thousands of <reading>こう</reading>いちs walking around, and they all stare at you (though they pretend like they aren't). Hmm, こういち doesn't seem to care, so everyone else in public doesn't seem to care either.

meaning_mnemonic: If you give a <radical>woman</radical> a <radical>machine</radical> she'll <kanji>begin</kanji> learning how to use it right away. She'll also get it to <kanji>start</kanji> before anyone else could. Women are really good at starting up machines!
reading_mnemonic: Actually, before she can <kanji>begin</kanji>, she has to shear the <reading>shee</reading>p (し) over there. The machine is going to turn wool into yarn, but you can't just start that process by shoving the sheep in there. You have to keep the little sheep safe!
extra_reading_mnemonic: (similar to 初) Right now it's time <kanji>to begin</kanji> <reading>Haj</reading> (はじ). (Haj is the fifth pillar of Islam, and is a pilgrimage to Mecca during the month of Dhu al-Hijja). You need to start Haj right now!

meaning_mnemonic: Let the <radical>sun</radical> shine into your <radical>ear</radical> while sitting on a <radical>stool</radical> and make sure <kanji>most</kanji> of it gets in your head. You want to fill your brain with the most sun anyone ever has.
reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Most</kanji> of this is for your <reading>cy</reading>borg (さい). You're testing out a new way to power it (its solar battery is near its ear/brain area), but if you can't get most of the sun into your ear, it won't be enough to power most of the cyborg's robo-parts.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 最も (もっとも) - Think of <kanji>the most</kanji> ridiculous <reading>motto</reading> (もっと) you've ever heard. Now imagine a motto that's even more ridiculous. Here are some actual totally real mottos that are the most ridiculous: "What Can Brown Do for You?" "It's Not for Women" "If It Doesn't Get All Over the Place, It Doesn't Belong in Your Face" and of course, "Why Not Enjoy the Go?"

meaning_mnemonic: You have <radical>spikes</radical> growing out of a <radical>sheep</radical> with <radical>fins</radical>. Turn this thing into a <kanji>business</kanji>! You could totally charge people money to look at it. Sure, you could also donate it to science, but a business-minded person like you knows a business opportunity when you see one. Step right up! Just five dollars for a glance at the rare spiky mer-sheep!
reading_mnemonic: As you evolve your <kanji>business</kanji>, you let customers feed the sheep <reading>gyo</reading>za (ぎょう) dumplings, its favorite snack. For a nominal fee, of course. People love it when the mutant sheep eats gyoza out of their hands. Wouldn't you?

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>tree</radical> marked with a <radical>yellow</radical> X on the <kanji>side</kanji> of the house is going to get cut down. You’ve marked it with a yellow X so the hired help knows which tree to cut down. The tree marked with a yellow X is the only one in danger of causing damage to your roof in the event of a storm.
reading_mnemonic: Wait, that woman with the chainsaw is <reading>Yoko</reading> (よこ) Ono! Yes, the same Yoko Ono who’s married to John Lennon of the Beatles. What’s she doing chopping down trees on the <kanji>side</kanji> of your house? Who can say. Silly Yoko.

meaning_mnemonic:
If a <radical>lip ring</radical> (or two in this case) is what you <radical>lack</radical>, it's going to be way easier for you to <kanji>sing</kanji> a <kanji>song</kanji>.

Imagine singing a song with a couple lip rings in your mouth. The articulation will be all wrong! It's definitely better to lack lip rings if you're going to sing.
reading_mnemonic: Where are you always singing <kanji>song</kanji>s, by the way? In your <reading>ca</reading>r (か). It's not just you, either. Pretty much everyone likes to sing in their car.
extra_reading_mnemonic: Think of <reading>Uta</reading> from One Piece. She loves <kanji>to sing</kanji>! She's really good at singing her <kanji>song</kanji>s (歌を歌う).

visually_similar_kanji: 球, 永, 氷, 水
meaning_mnemonic: Look at the <radical>ground</radical>! You spilled some <radical>water</radical> <radical>drop</radical>s, so I <kanji>request</kanji> that you wipe them up. I'd do it myself, but you're the one who spilled them, so I'm requesting that you do it. Pretty reasonable request, right?
reading_mnemonic: Oh, one more thing. I <kanji>request</kanji> that you wipe up the water with this <reading>cu</reading>cumber (きゅう). Weird request, but ok.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 求める (もとめる) - What is it that you want (<kanji>to want something</kanji>)? You want a <reading>moat</reading> (もと) around your home. Your neighbor's cats keep pooping on your lawn, but if you had a moat they wouldn't be able to get to your lawn in the first place, since cats hate water (and alligators). You request a moat (<kanji>to request</kanji>)!

meaning_mnemonic:
(A <radical>tsunami</radical> that is <radical>Chinese</radical> is located in the <kanji>Chinese</kanji> land of <kanji>China</kanji>!)

~~~A <radical>tsunami</radical> hit ancient <radical>China</radical> and formed the <kanji>Chinese</kanji> country we know now as... <kanji>China</kanji>!

Sometimes this kanji also means <kanji>man</kanji>. In fact, it used to refer specifically to people of the Han dynasty, but over time evolved into a term for men in specific contexts.
