reading_mnemonic: But where did that geoduck come from? As you turn from the cliff edge, you find yourself <kanji>face</kanji>-to-face with a <reading>cow</reading> (かお). This cow is the one who hit you in the face with a geoduck. You don't know why, but something about your face has upset the cow.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 顔面 (がんめん) - You stare at the cow's <kanji>face</kanji>, but then the cow face disappears. It becomes totally <reading>gone</reading> (がん). It reminds you of an urban legend of the gone men. They say if a man that is walking up to you with no face, it is a man with a gone face. Those men are men who are a part of the gone men (がんめん). Faces, totally gone!

meaning_mnemonic: You can <radical>eat</radical> solids all you want, but you'll still <radical>lack</radical> liquids to <kanji>drink</kanji>. You can't live just from eating, you have to drink things too!
reading_mnemonic: You get desperate for a <kanji>drink</kanji> and put some <reading>no</reading>ri (の) seaweed in a blender, trying to create a drink of your own. <reading>NO</reading>! We need to get a real drink!
extra_reading_mnemonic: 飲酒 (いんしゅ) - Where's a good place for (drinking alcohol)? An <reading>inn</reading> (いん), of course!

meaning_mnemonic: When the <radical>mouth</radical> of a <radical>bird</radical> opens, you're most likely to hear a <kanji>chirp</kanji>. This is how birds communicate. They open their mouths and let out a series of chirps. Chirp chirp chirp!
reading_mnemonic:
The best way to experience the <kanji>chirp</kanji>-chirping of birds is to offer them <reading>na</reading>chos (な). Birds love nachos so much, it's a guaranteed way to make them chirp with delight.

Picture yourself surrounded by birds of all kinds, handing out nachos. Just listen to their happy chirping. They're sitting on your arms, shoulders, and even your head, trying to get closer to the nachos.

You hear a lot of birds chirping more during the month of <reading>May</reading> (めい).

meaning_mnemonic: In <radical>prison</radical>, <radical>Wolverine</radical> gets picked on for the <radical>barb</radical>s coming out of his hands. This creates a lot of <kanji>conflict</kanji> between him and the other prisoners. They don't take kindly to mutants, and Wolverine doesn't take kindly to bigots — hence the conflict.
reading_mnemonic: This constant <kanji>conflict</kanji> between Wolverine and the other inmates is really affecting his <reading>sou</reading>l (そう). Despite what people think, Wolverine really doesn't like to fight. He just hates injustice so much, he feels he has to do something about it.
extra_reading_mnemonic: Wolverine is starting <kanji>to compete</kanji> and <kanji>to argue</kanji> with someone, who is yelling at him: "You <reading>are so</reading> (あらそ) stupid!". You might want to imagine this in an accent that gets you closer to the Japanese pronunciation.

meaning_mnemonic: If you know the radical meaning <radical>orders</radical> you know the kanji meaning <kanji>orders</kanji> as well!
reading_mnemonic: Your <kanji>orders</kanji> are to get a <reading>ray</reading> (れい) gun. The authority figure orders you to find a ray gun, I guess to prepare for battle?

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>leader</radical> who takes the <radical>middle</radical> of the road on every issue is likely to have an average <kanji>relationship</kanji> with everyone. He doesn't really take sides in matters, and just stays in the middle. This makes him seem like a wishy-washy people-pleaser, and as such he's only able to maintain average, mid-tier relationships.
reading_mnemonic:
Also, this kanji is pronounced exactly like the vocab word <reading>中</reading> (なか). If you can remember that, it'll make remembering 仲 easier.

~~~Imagine a flip-flopping politician you have an average <kanji>relationship</kanji> with. Now imagine that there's a <reading>knocker</reading> (なか) on their forehead and you get to knock that knocker as hard as you like. Maybe you can knock some integrity into them and form a better relationship.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> has a <radical>cloud</radical> that he uses to <kanji>transmit</kanji> all of the messages he needs to send to his people. The cloud floats above him and when he wants to tell people something he just whispers into the cloud and it transmits his message really, really loudly to all of them.
reading_mnemonic:
As the leader <kanji>transmit</kanji>s his latest series of messages to you and the others, you notice a pretty large <reading>den</reading>t (でん) in it. That dent is probably a clue to what this cloud is really made of.

It's probably just a speaker attached to a drone covered in cotton balls.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
You want <kanji>to convey</kanji> your knowledge to your apprentice, so you make them the best <reading>two ta</reading>cos (つた) you've ever made. They just wanted you <kanji>to tell</kanji> them the recipe, but you believe showing it is a better way <kanji>to pass down</kanji> that skill.

つて - When you get someone to transmit information, they're a type of <kanji>intermediary</kanji>, a <kanji>go-between</kanji>, if you will. When the go-between gets back and is about to tell you everything the other group said, it takes him <reading>two takes</reading> (つて) to get it all right. The other group had a lot to say and he had trouble getting it all on the first take, but he totally nailed it on the second.

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>leader</radical> <radical>stand</radical>s at the highest <kanji>rank</kanji> in an organization. The leader is of the highest rank and stands above all others.
reading_mnemonic: This great leader is actually the leader of the boy scouts. And as we all know, the highest <kanji>rank</kanji> in boy scouts is the rank of <reading>ea</reading>gle (い) scout. This great leader has attained the rank of eagle scout and stands above all other scouts.

visually_similar_kanji: 邸, 抵, 底, 紙
meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> of your <radical>clan</radical> wants to live close to the <radical>ground</radical> so he demands you get <kanji>low</kanji>. Low, low, with your belly to the ground. That way you're always below him, since he's the leader.
reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Low</kanji> people like you can only eat low food like potatoes. But that's boring, so you low people learned to make <reading>ta</reading>ter (てい) tots. You roll them to each other and eat them without lifting your heads.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
He low but he coo' because he likes tater tots.

低い (ひくい) - You look down and very <kanji>low</kanji> to the ground is a man, looking up at you. Your friend is there too, but you don't know this little man. Your friend says "<reading>He coo</reading>', he coo," referring to the low to the ground man.

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>leader</radical> is searching the <radical>ground</radical> of the <radical>rice paddy</radical> for <radical>treasure</radical>. It is said that this treasure here in this rice field will make things much easier for the leader (that's what leaders really want, after all). If she gets this treasure, it will be a great <kanji>convenience</kanji> for her, because convenience is everything when you're the leader.
reading_mnemonic: She finds a place to dig in the ground. It looks like there's some fresh dirt here. Finally, the treasure of <kanji>convenience</kanji> that will make this leader's life so much easier. She digs into the ground and pulls out a box. When she opens it, she finds out it's a <reading>ben</reading>to (べん). "My god," she thinks. "This really will make my life more convenient. My people can take their lunches with them now instead of coming back to base to eat, which will waste way less time!"
extra_reading_mnemonic:
Maybe you'll have to throw a bento in the bin?

郵便 (ゆうびん) - You get a lot of junk <kanji>mail</kanji>, so you throw it in the waste <reading>bin</reading> (びん). The waste bin is where that junk mail goes. 郵便: Mail (or post) has convenience because it is sent for you in the mail (or the post!).

meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>leader</radical> makes you lift <radical>heavy</radical> loads with all your <radical>power</radical>, since this is what you do for <kanji>work</kanji>. Why do you do this kind of work? Well, you're good at it and the leader makes you do it, I guess.
reading_mnemonic: Where do you get the power to do all this <kanji>work</kanji>? From <reading>dou</reading>ghnuts (どう). You eat nothing but doughnuts. If you had no doughnuts, you couldn't work. In fact, your leader pays you for your work… in doughnuts.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 働く (はたらく) - The kanji itself means <kanji>work</kanji>, and the verb version means <kanji>to work</kanji>, <kanji>to labor</kanji>, and sometimes <kanji>to commit</kanji> (a crime). If you are as mad as a <reading>hatter</reading> (はたら) you'll need to work very hard to regain your sanity. You know The Hatter from Alice in Wonderland? Imagine how hard he would have to work to be considered "normal".

meaning_mnemonic: The card game fish are best at is <radical>blackjack</radical> (or <radical>flowers in the ground</radical>) because they can easily hold the cards with their <radical>fins</radical> <kanji>together</kanji>. In blackjack you don't have to have a huge hand, full of cards. It's just a few, so fish fins can keep them together and just hit or stay.
reading_mnemonic: Once a year trillions of fish get <kanji>together</kanji> in <reading>きょう</reading>と to play blackjack. They have a huge tournament there once a year.

meaning_mnemonic: You wear a special <radical>outfit</radical> and equip a <radical>sword</radical> whenever you do something for the <kanji>first</kanji> time. Doing something for the first time is always scary, but the right outfit and a sword at your side can give you the confidence and courage to overcome your jitters!
reading_mnemonic: So, what is it you're doing for the <kanji>first</kanji> time? A fashion <reading>show</reading> (しょ). Your special outfit and sword aren't just to calm your nerves — they're also what you'll be showing off on the catwalk.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
Hold onto your hats when you're going to Haj or a fashion show.

初めて - "What are you beginning? You are beginning <reading>Haj</reading> (はじ). (Haj is the fifth pillar of Islam, and is a pilgrimage to Mecca during the month of Dhu al-Hijja)." You know that 初 means "first" This word means <kanji>for the first time</kanji>. Think of めて as "meet." Then think "when we met for the first time ____ happened."

初恋 (はつこい) - First love is wild, so be sure to hold onto your <reading>hats</reading> (はつ)!

meaning_mnemonic: In your <radical>mouth</radical> you put a <radical>sword</radical> and a <radical>knife</radical>. Now that you have them in there, you have to make them <kanji>separate</kanji> from each other.
reading_mnemonic: Why are you trying to make a sword and knife <kanji>separate</kanji> in your mouth? Because someone <reading>bets</reading> (べつ) you can't do it.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 別れる (わかれる) - The kanji itself means <kanji>separate</kanji>, so you can guess the meaning is <kanji>to separate</kanji> or <kanji>to be divided</kanji>. You won the bet, so your reward is a car. You say "<reading>Wa, ca</reading>r (わか)?!"

meaning_mnemonic: Cut <radical>grain</radical>s with a <radical>knife</radical> to make them smaller and you'll make a great <kanji>profit</kanji>. By cutting them, now you can get three grains worth of money for what was once a single grain.
reading_mnemonic: To make an even better <kanji>profit</kanji>, you decide to cut up <reading>ree</reading>ds (り) too. You stuff the grains in the reeds and sell that as "self-cooking" sets.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
利く (きく) - What works so well? Your special <reading>key</reading> (き) that can unlock anyone and anything's potential. Imagine putting it into a key slot in someone's back. Someone who's a good for nothing can't-do-anything is now an effective member of society! Go around using your key on other non-effective things and show them that anything is possible!

You know the kanji means <kanji>profit</kanji>. When you make it into a verb, though, it means <kanji>to work well</kanji>. If you think about it, when something works well it makes you a profit.

meaning_mnemonic: Using your <radical>construction</radical> <radical>power</radical> you build something great. A true <kanji>achievement</kanji> built for the achievement of making kanji learning easier (like this kanji-organizer web app)!
reading_mnemonic: This <kanji>achievement</kanji> was made possible by <reading>こう</reading>いち, so of course this construction project also includes a giant statue of the man himself. What an achievement of a kanji-organizer web app. What an achievement of a statue. What an achievement of an achievement.

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> sits on a <radical>stool</radical> to conserve her <radical>power</radical>, as she <kanji>toil</kanji>s away in the kitchen. She toils away preparing a feast.
reading_mnemonic: She also <kanji>toil</kanji>s for her <reading>do</reading>g (ど). Anything the dog wants, the dog gets. That means double the toil for her. But hey, at least her dog is cute.

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>Viking</radical> needs a lot of <radical>power</radical> to <kanji>labor</kanji> in the fields. Only the strong can do labor.
reading_mnemonic: It takes a lot of <kanji>labor</kanji> to harvest <reading>roe</reading> (ろう), but that’s what the Viking loves to eat! Vikings power through labor for roe. Roe is delicious, but it’s small and delicate.

meaning_mnemonic: In your <radical>mouth</radical> there is a <radical>jet</radical> dropping <kanji>flavor</kanji> bombs. Every time you <kanji>taste</kanji> something, it's actually because a tiny jet has flown into your mouth to bomb you with flavor.
reading_mnemonic: And what has more <kanji>flavor</kanji> than a big slab of <reading>me</reading>at (み)? You love meat and its flavor nearly as much as you love the <kanji>taste</kanji> of its juice. So many good things to put in your mouth!
extra_reading_mnemonic: You may have the ability to <kanji>taste</kanji> things now, but just wait until you get up there in <reading>age</reading> (あじ). You'll find that the tastes and flavors you once liked will become bland, and you'll need a lot of sauces like Sriracha to make things taste better.

meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Orders</radical> coming from your <radical>mouth</radical> will determine the <kanji>fate</kanji> of your soldiers. You are their commanding officer and your orders determine their <kanji>life</kanji> and death.
reading_mnemonic: You are the commanding officer on the <reading>May</reading>flower (めい). You give orders to colonize America. The orders spewing from your mouth hole determine the <kanji>fate</kanji> of the settlers and the fate of America and the fate of the world! You and the Mayflower have changed everything forever.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
The Book of <reading>Enoch</reading> (いのち) has passed down your fate and told you how to use your <kanji>life</kanji>. You must read the book of Enoch and find out what you're supposed to do.

寿命 (じゅみょう) - When you think of a <kanji>lifespan</kanji>, think of how that affects everyone. Me, you... well, just those things. Combine them both into <reading>myou</reading> (みょう). That is who the lifespan affects. Myou!

meaning_mnemonic: There is a <radical>woman</radical> and a <radical>child</radical> in front of you. You <kanji>like</kanji> them very much.

extra_reading_mnemonic:
You like your こういちs and Sue, but 子? No!

好き (すき) - Who do you <kanji>like</kanji> more than anyone? Your friend <reading>Sue</reading>. If you know someone named Sue, pretend you like her. If you don't, think of a famous person you know named Sue and use her, pretending you're good friends that like each other a lot.

好む (このむ) - What’s something easy <kanji>to be fond of</kanji>? <reading>子</reading>? <reading>No</reading> (この), not for you. You’re always saying “子? No!” Most people are fond of kids, at least their own, but not you. Noisy, germy, needy 子? No, no thank you!

meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>mountain</radical> on top of the <radical>cliff</radical> is <radical>dry</radical> from the <kanji>coast</kanji> below. Just from looking at the raging <kanji>shore</kanji> below, you'd think everything would be wet, it's splashing everywhere!

You're on top of the mountain and the entire coast is stretching out below. The shore goes as far as your eyes can see.
reading_mnemonic:
Sitting up there, watching the <kanji>coast</kanji> with you, is <reading>Gan</reading>dhi (がん). The world famous Gandhi, is just hanging out up here with you, looking down at what you now realize must be a coast in India.

Sit down next to Gandhi and close your eyes. You can hear the water hitting the shore below. The coastal birds are screaming. You crack open an eye and see Gandhi still sitting perfectly still.

meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>sound</radical> of your <radical>heart</radical> gives me an <kanji>idea</kanji>. The methodic thump thump thumping of a heart puts me in a trance that gives me great ideas. It’s a very inspirational sound, the sound of a heart is. It gives me an idea.

Alternatively, you could look at this kanji and see a "stand" radical and something that kind of (almost) looks like the kanji for "think." When you stand up and think, you come up with your very own <kanji>idea</kanji>s!
reading_mnemonic: The heart of an <reading>ea</reading>gle (い) is very strong. The person who knew this probably came up with the <kanji>idea</kanji> to make the bald eagle a symbol of the United States. Eagles are always flying around and doing things, so their hearts are very strong.

meaning_mnemonic: When a <radical>drunkard</radical> holds a <radical>sword</radical>, it <kanji>becomes</kanji> something else. The drunkard doesn't become a swordsman, they're still just a drunkard. But the sword in their hands does.
reading_mnemonic: The sword has <kanji>become</kanji> a <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい)! They say that in the right hands, the sword evolves into a saber. But why did it choose this drunkard?
extra_reading_mnemonic:
The dude is starting <kanji>to become something</kanji> else. He's transforming, but he's not sure into what. First, he gets fins... Uh oh, something in the water. Then, he gains a tail and rubbery skin... Hmm, something sea mammal-like. Oh, and then a huge horn sprouts out of his face. He's going to become a <reading>na</reading>rwhal (な). 

There's a war going on amongst narwhals, and the saber is trying to recruit narwhals.

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>simple</radical> <radical>drunkard</radical> starting a <kanji>war</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic:
The simple drunkard started a <kanji>war</kanji> with the <reading>cen</reading>taurs (せん)! This is especially unfortunate, because the centaurs are really good at <kanji>battle</kanji>s because they're all automatically cavalry troops.

Imagine the war: humans vs centaurs. Tens of thousands clashing in battle.
extra_reading_mnemonic: In a fierce <kanji>fight</kanji> / <kanji>battle</kanji> / <kanji>conflict</kanji>, there's always a lot of collateral damage. One of the things that gets destroyed is your car. But you can't do anything about it, it's battle time! So you wave goodbye to your car saying, "<reading>Ta-ta ca</reading>r (たたか)!" as you punch some jerk in the face.

meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>fingers</radical> always seem to <radical>suit</radical> the random things you <kanji>pick up</kanji> off the ground. (An old thimble. A discarded onion ring. A dead worm you tie in a knot.) Your incredible fingers suit them beautifully, almost as if they were jewelry, so of course you pick up all of them.
reading_mnemonic: You're walking around looking for something to <kanji>pick up</kanji> when you see a sword in a rock. Yes, this will suit you. You pick up the sword and people jump out around you and tell you that you are the new <reading>hero</reading> (ひろ)! Uh oh. Maybe you shouldn't have picked this up.

meaning_mnemonic: If you use your <radical>fingers</radical> to <radical>spoon</radical> out some of the <radical>sun</radical>, you'll come back with just one <kanji>finger</kanji>. Ouch!
reading_mnemonic:
Don't worry, you aren't the only one out there with just one <kanji>finger</kanji>, <reading>shee</reading>p (し) only have one finger too. I mean, they're hooves, which are really just a single animal finger. It's just big and kind of flat.

Picture sitting with a sheep. It's right across from you, staring into your eyes. It reaches out its sheep finger hoof and you reach out with your finger. They touch. It's magical.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
You be with your sheep friend and dodging saws.

What do you use your <kanji>finger</kanji> for the most? For pointing, of course! Imagine going up to people and saying, "What will <reading>you be</reading> (ゆび) when you grow up?" Point your finger at the next person, "What will you be?" Keep going until you're just saying, "You be? You be?" with your finger out.

指す (さす) - The kanji means finger. So, if you "to finger" something, what are you doing? You're pointing. That's why this word means <kanji>to point</kanji>. You are pointing at something in fear. It is a <reading>saw</reading> (さ). You don't want to get hurt by the saw (saws are known for sawing off fingers), so you point to put attention on it so everyone is careful.

meaning_mnemonic: As the year starts moving in the <radical>direction</radical> of <radical>winter</radical>, the trees must <kanji>release</kanji> their leaves.
reading_mnemonic: The trees <kanji>release</kanji> all of their leaves onto your <reading>ho</reading>me (ほう). Slowly, you watch in shock as your home is covered by the released leaves. They enter in through the windows, doors, and the chimney.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
放す (はなす) - You need <kanji>to release</kanji> your pet <reading>花</reading> (はな). It's a monstrous, carnivorous 花 that you keep in a cage in your backyard. You think it's super cute, but your neighbors say it scares them, so you need <kanji>to set free</kanji> your beloved 花. Hopefully it doesn't eat anyone on its way back to the wild.

放す often suggests that you've released something in a way that gives it freedom to move or go where it wants. Think of letting your dog run in the field — it's not just that you let go of the leash, but that the dog is now free to run around as it pleases.

Your feet are all sweaty from being out in the sun, and walking on this dirt road gives you <reading>muck ashi</reading> (むかし). Your ashi (feet) are all mucky and muddy from the combination of dirt and sweat. Your muck ashi are really gross, man.

The waves are basically punching you in the gut, forcing the air out of your lungs, and making you shout HA!
extra_reading_mnemonic: You jump on a <kanji>wave</kanji> and ride around the world on it. As you ride this wave, it gets bigger and bigger, until it reaches tsu<reading>nami</reading> (なみ) proportions. Imagine looking down from the tsunami at the vast, blue sea all around you. That's quite a wave you're riding.

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>tsunami</radical> <radical>master</radical> has the power to <kanji>pour</kanji> water wherever he pleases. Tsunami masters are masters over the most powerful water force in the universe, so it makes sense that they have the ability to pour water at will, wherever they please. Best not tick off the master, unless you want a tsunami poured on your head.
reading_mnemonic: If <reading>Chew</reading>bacca (ちゅう) was trying to attack you, you’d be able to defend yourself easily. Simply ask a tsunami master to <kanji>pour</kanji> on him and Chewbacca would surrender in a heartbeat. Chewbacca doesn’t like having water poured on him, especially not all the water from a tsunami.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 注ぐ (そそぐ) - You are going <kanji>to pour</kanji> some <reading>sauce</reading> (そそ). On Chewbacca and on your food.

meaning_mnemonic:
This <radical>tsunami</radical> is ridden by a <radical>sheep</radical> in classic <kanji>Western style</kanji>. And by Western style I mean the sheep is dressed in a cowboy outfit and has put a saddle atop the tsunami wave to ride it. It's a tsunami rodeo and this crazy sheep is riding that tsunami wave in classic Western style.

This kanji also means <kanji>ocean</kanji>, because presumably the people from the West, with their Western style, came from across the ocean. You'll want to be familiar with both meanings for vocab later on.
reading_mnemonic: After a whole day of riding this tsunami, the sheep is hankerin' for some <kanji>Western-style</kanji> food, namely <reading>yo</reading>gurt (よう). Yogurt is Western-style food, right? If it helps you can imagine the yogurt is flavored like apple pie, to make it more American and Western.

extra_reading_mnemonic:
薦める - This has the same reading as 勧める (<reading>すす</reading>める), since they mean almost the same thing. The kanji itself means <kanji>recommend</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabkanjilary>to recommend</kanji>. This word is often used in a positive context for recommending things, actions, and people by implying or pointing out their charms, merits, or both.

Although 薦める and 勧める are similar, there are subtle differences between the two. 勧める is often used to suggest that someone perform a specific action, often as friendly advice or encouragement. It can also be used when offering something, such as a drink. On the other hand, 薦める is used to recommend a person or thing as suitable for a particular situation, with a focus on endorsing the subject rather than a specific action.

貴い - This has the same reading as 尊い (revered, noble), so if you remember that, you can read 貴い too! In case you forgot, here's a mnemonic to help you: How can you tell if someone comes from a <kanji>noble</kanji> background? Just check their <reading>toe toe</reading> (とうと). Most noble families are pretty inbred, so a lot of their members will have a big toe (the long とう) with another small toe growing out of it (short と). This is a common birth defect among inbred aristocrats.

While 尊い is used for things you honor from the heart, 貴い leans toward a dignified, noble kind of value — the kind tied to high status or social rank. Because of that, you may encounter 貴い in stories about historical class systems or old social hierarchies. It doesn't appear as commonly as 尊い in modern Japanese, but you may still see it in descriptions of someone's noble presence or the sense of dignity they give off.

The kanji itself means <kanji>char</kanji>, but the verb version is <kanji>to get burned</kanji>, <kanji>to get scorched</kanji>, or <kanji>to get charred</kanji>.

焦がす means to burn the surface of something, usually blackening it to some degree. Unlike 焦げる, it can be for both intentional burning (a nice crème brûlée) and accidental burning (leaving bread in the toaster too long, scorching your sleeve on the stove). Remember how 焦げる means "to get burned"? 焦がす is the transitive version, so this time someone is actively doing the burning, making it <kanji>to burn</kanji>, <kanji>to scorch</kanji>, or <kanji>to char</kanji>.

焦る is a bit of a weird word. The kanji is <kanji>char</kanji>, and a previous word you learned (焦げる) is "to be burned." This, on the other hand, is "to be in a hurry" or "to be impatient." You can tell that this is that word because it only has one kana, る, which stands for <reading>ru</reading>de. 擦る (<kanji>To Rub</kanji>) vs. 擦れる (<kanji>To Be Rubbed</kanji>).

擦る (する / こする) - The kanji itself means <kanji>rub</kanji> and this verb means <kanji>to rub</kanji> or <kanji>to scrub</kanji>. The <reading>cos</reading>t  (こす) of your rubbing actions will be high. So this word has two readings and both mean “to rub.” But you usually use する for a single action, such as lighting a match or grazing your knee, while こする means doing it repeatedly, like when you’re cleaning or polishing something.

擦れる (すれる / こすれる) - This is an intransitive version of 擦る, so it means <kanji>to be rubbed</kanji>. It often implies damage, in which case it can mean <kanji>to be grazed</kanji> or <kanji>to be scraped</kanji>, like when your knee gets grazed against a rough wall. You really don’t want your knee <kanji>to be grazed</kanji>. If it happens, you are gonna <reading>sue</reading> (す). extra_reading_mnemonic: 朗らか (ほがらか) - Of all the people who are <kanji>bright</kanji> and <kanji>cheerful</kanji>, one man comes to mind. The cheerful Hulk <reading>Hoga</reading>n (ほが). He's smiling with the roe and good moon too.

meaning_mnemonic:
You've been ordered to <radical>spear</radical> this <radical>tree</radical> but you decide to be really <kanji>gentle</kanji> instead.

Imagine gently poking the tree with your spear. You glance around nervously, hoping no one notices how easy on it you're being.
reading_mnemonic: You're being really <kanji>gentle</kanji> to the tree when a <reading>jewel</reading> (じゅう) falls out of its branches and hits you on the head. The jewel has a little note on it, "Thank you for being gentle." Did... did the tree just reward you for being gentle?!
extra_reading_mnemonic:
A tree giving you a jewel? That's <reading>new</reading> (にゅう) to you.

柔らかい (やわらかい) - The kanji means <kanji>gentle</kanji>, and the adjective version means <kanji>soft</kanji> — as in a gentle, <kanji>tender</kanji> kind of softness. Think soft towel, soft hand, soft voice… anything soft in a way that gives you the warm fuzzies. In reference to the human body, 柔らかい can also mean <kanji>flexible</kanji>, with an emphasis on supple, effortless movement.

You find something that is so <kanji>soft</kanji> to the touch. You touch it. You can't stop. The monkey you're touching tells you to stop. It doesn't like to be touched. But, you won't stop. "<reading>Yah wha</reading>t (やわ) you gonna do about it, monkey?" "<reading>Yah, wha</reading>t can I do, I guess," replies the monkey.

meaning_mnemonic: If a <radical>tsunami</radical> hits a <radical>pirate</radical> they are going to <kanji>sink</kanji> no matter how good of a pirate captain they are.
reading_mnemonic: As the tsunami comes to <kanji>sink</kanji> the pirate, the pirate holds his <reading>chin</reading> (ちん) up high. He will die with dignity.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
沈む (<kanji>To Sink</kanji>) vs. 沈める (<kanji>To Sink Something</kanji>).

沈む (しずむ) - The kanji itself means <kanji>sink</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <kanji>to sink</kanji>. Your boat is about <kanji>to sink</kanji>, so you run around yelling, "<reading>She's</reading> (しず) sinking! She's… she's sinking! Abandon ship!" Boats are always female, so be careful not to say "it." If you don't say "she's" sinking, your crew might not get the message.

On a literal level, 沈む refers to physical sinking — a boat sinking into the water or someone's foot sinking into the mud, for example. However, it can also be used metaphorically to talk about things like the sun setting (太陽が沈む), a nation falling into decline (国が沈む), or even someone "sinking" into a depressed mood (気分が沈む).

沈める (しずめる) - The kanji itself means <kanji>sink</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <kanji>to sink something</kanji> or <kanji>to submerge something</kanji>. When you sink something, like a battleship, you go on and say: "<reading>she's</reading> (しず) sunk, I sunk her." That's like your tagline, or something. You say it for some reason because you think it's cool.

This is a transitive verb, meaning it takes a direct object. So instead of describing something sinking on its own, you use 沈める when you sink an enemy ship or submerge yourself in a bathtub. You know this because you can't sink anything until you get that mail (める) saying, "Yes, proceed with sinking!" You've got to have that mail if you want to sink something, or else everyone will blame you for the missing ship — or for you disappearing under the water.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>spring</radical> <radical>water</radical> always puts you at <kanji>peace</kanji>. Everything from winter is melting and trickling and thawing. All the dripping sounds fill you with a peace you can barely describe.
reading_mnemonic: You want to feel this <kanji>peace</kanji> all the time, not just in spring, so you dip your <reading>tie</reading> (たい) in the spring water. Now your tie is making the peaceful dripping sounds you love.

meaning_mnemonic: You're struck by a <radical>tsunami</radical>, mauled by a <radical>canine</radical>, and then set on <radical>fire</radical>. It seems the universe is trying to <kanji>destroy</kanji> you. A tsunami, a canine attack, and a fire disaster make for quite a triple-whammy.
reading_mnemonic:

Imagine pulling on your Mets jersey only to suddenly receive a tsunami warning on your phone. Then, you hear a canine growling and catch a whiff of something burning nearby. Uh-oh, the universe is trying to destroy you again!
extra_reading_mnemonic:
滅びる (ほろびる) - The kanji itself means <kanji>destroy</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <kanji>to be destroyed</kanji>. You know you're not destroying things because of the beer (びる). You'd never destroy beer... but someone else might. Grrr. "THE <reading>HORROR</reading>!" (ほろ) you cry, as your beer (びる) is about <vocabulary>to be destroyed</vocabulary>.

滅ぼす (<kanji>To Destroy</kanji>) vs. 滅びる (<kanji>To Be Destroyed</kanji>).

radical_characters: 氵, 丷, 一, 幺
meaning_mnemonic: A (fresh water) <radical>tsunami</radical>. Some <radical>horns</radical>. The <radical>ground</radical>. A bunch of <radical>poop</radical>. Combine these together and let them decompose a while. You'll have yourself some very <kanji>nourishing</kanji> soil.
reading_mnemonic:
This is the kind of <kanji>nourishing</kanji> soil that <reading>Je</reading>sus (じ) would make if he was into making soil, probably.

Imagine him making soil made out of those things. Jesus approves of this nourishing soil.

meaning_mnemonic:

The moon does affect the tides a bit, so you can imagine the tsunami as the water getting bigger whenever the moon is out. That's just the tide.
reading_mnemonic:
You go check out the <kanji>tide</kanji>. The water is coming in a little stronger, and something washes up on the shore. It's a body! You roll the body over and it is Mrs. <reading>Chou</reading> (ちょう)!

She wakes up and says, "If only you came at low tide then I would never have been saved!" She jumps up and runs off, yelling something about destroying the world.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 潮 - If you think of the <kanji>tide</kanji>, you think of the ocean. If you think of the ocean and what it's filled with (besides water) you think of <reading>salt</reading> (しお).

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>fire</radical> <radical>door</radical> is a door that leads to something full of fire. That thing is a <kanji>furnace</kanji>. Open the fire door and feel the heat of the furnace. Hot!
reading_mnemonic: You're using the <kanji>furnace</kanji> to melt tar to put on the <reading>ro</reading>ad (ろ). Smell the tar baking from the furnace. Feel the heat from the furnace. Fix the road, while you're at it.

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>cow</radical> in the <radical>winter</radical> doesn't like to leave the barn to go to the <kanji>pasture</kanji>. It has to, though, because a cow's gotta eat.
reading_mnemonic: ぼく is one of the common ways to say "I" in Japanese (which you should remember!). In this case, you're a boy... a cowboy, and you say, "<reading>ぼく</reading>will take these cows out to <kanji>pasture</kanji>!"

visually_similar_kanji: 修, 診, 参, 惨
meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>king</radical>'s <radical>hat</radical>, not to mention the <radical>hair</radical> stuck to said hat, is incredibly <kanji>rare</kanji>. If you have your hands on either of these things, you'll be a rich duck.
reading_mnemonic: Then you look closer at the hat. It's about to get even <kanji>rare</kanji>r. Attached to the hair is the king's <reading>chin</reading> (ちん). The king only had one chin, so that's about as rare as they come.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 珍しい (めずらしい) - What's the adjective form of <kanji>rare</kanji>? It's <kanji>rare</kanji>. But, this can also mean <kanji>unusual</kanji> or <kanji>curious</kanji> (as in "odd" curious, not that you're curious about something). You know what's <kanji>rare</kanji> and <kanji>unusual</kanji>? People who pronounce measurable as "<reading>mezura</reading>ble" (めずら). They're a <vocabulary>curious</vocabulary> bunch, and they're pretty rare, but they exist.

meaning_mnemonic:
Two <radical>king</radical>s are here right <radical>now</radical>! We need to entertain them otherwise who knows what they'll do. Get out the <kanji>harp</kanji>, or the <kanji>zither</kanji>, or something.

Kinda like Double D from Ed, Edd n Eddy, but he's playing a different instrument (pedal steel guitar) which is kindof but not exactly a zither.
reading_mnemonic:
You may already know that a Japanese <kanji>harp</kanji> is called a <reading>こと</reading>, but here's a mnemonic to help you if you don't:

When playing your <kanji>harp</kanji>, you always wear your <reading>coat</reading> (こと).

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>bamboo</radical> stalk looks the <radical>same</radical> as a big ol' <kanji>cylinder</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic: Picture a <kanji>cylinder</kanji> shaped <reading>とう</reading>きょう. All the buildings are cylinders. The city itself is cylinder shaped too. Even... gasp! The people of とうきょう! とうきょう is a really weird city now that they passed the cylinder law.

When it comes to <kanji>pipe</kanji>s, you always want to have two sets of two of them, just in case. So, that's a <reading>two two</reading> (つつ) set of pipes, lined up next to each other for backup.

meaning_mnemonic:

School registers, family registers, member registers — you name it. Picture the fields and hillsides back then, full of names scraped into the dirt.
reading_mnemonic:
If your name is in a <kanji>register</kanji>, people will find you very <reading>sexy</reading> (せき). This was true long ago too. There's nothing sexier than someone whose existence is accounted for in official documentation.

No wonder people went to the trouble of plowing their names into the dirt back then. They understood the sex appeal of registers.

meaning_mnemonic: When a <radical>yakuza</radical> takes a <radical>knife</radical> to <radical>clothes</radical>, it will of course cause a <kanji>split</kanji> or <kanji>tear</kanji>. Any knife (especially from a yakuza) will cause a split or tear in clothes.

裂く (<kanji>To Tear</kanji>) vs. 裂ける (<kanji>To Be Split</kanji>).

In order to get it open, you need <kanji>to tear</kanji> and rip it open with a <reading>saw</reading> (さ).

reading_mnemonic:

extra_reading_mnemonic: 襲う (おそう) - "You going <kanji>to attack</kanji> me or something? <reading>Oh so</reading> scary you are. Oh so scary. Ho ho ho." SHOE KICK!

meaning_mnemonic:

reading_mnemonic: The added <kanji>charm</kanji> of this game is that there's this big <reading>chu</reading>te (しゅ) at the end. It's so charming because you love chutes. You slide down the big chute!
extra_reading_mnemonic: 趣 (おもむき) - This word covers a lot of meanings so it can be <kanji>charm</kanji>, <kanji>taste</kanji>, <kanji>vibe</kanji>, or even <kanji>gist</kanji>. If something has <kanji>charm</kanji>, your thought/思 (<reading>おも</reading>) goes in that direction/向き (<reading>むき</reading>).  You feel the vibe? Do you get the gist?

露 (つゆ) - <kanji>Dew</kanji> is just the earth's way of giving water <reading>to you</reading> (つゆ). Rain is too forceful, you may not go to the ocean or a lake, so the earth gives dew to you by putting it on the grass outside your house everyday!

披露 (ひろう) - Sometimes, you can see some <reading>roe</reading> (ろう) in the dew. Life finds a way.

meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>axe</radical> is stuck into the <radical>ground</radical> on a <kanji>hill</kanji>. Imagine climbing up the hill, seeing the top of the hill with an axe on the ground.

meaning_mnemonic:

reading_mnemonic: The reading is <reading>samurai</reading> (さむらい), which should be easy enough to remember.

meaning_mnemonic:

(You have a sword that has a drop of something on it. That drop is a drop of blood. Sure, a sword will cut someone to spill some blood, but all you really need is any kind of blade to cut someone. Sword, knife, whatever, as long as it's a blade.)

reading_mnemonic: What were you doing wrong that caused me to <kanji>scold</kanji> you? You were feeding the 鹿 (<reading>しか</reading>). If you feed them they'll never be able to feed themselves!

meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>good luck</radical> radical and the <kanji>good luck</kanji> kanji are the same!

(This is the samurai radical on top of the mouth radical. If you get to hear what a samurai says, you'll have really good luck. Samurai are pretty hard to find nowadays, which is probably why my luck has been so bad...)

meaning_mnemonic:

How do you think the とうきょう tower came to be, anyway? It was once a big flower tower. They just replaced it with metal later. BOOM! History bomb, you're welcome.

Just imagine a princess saying "UGH, I'm just like a servant, I have to do all the crap you tell me." Then, all the servants roll their eyes, because, really, she's a princess, lucky duck.
reading_mnemonic:

~~~ The <kanji>princess</kanji> goes on to do whatever she wants. She tells the real servants, "Don't tell my daddy, the king, I did this. <reading>He may</reading> (ひめ) not like it."

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> uses her <radical>catapult</radical> for some good ol' fashioned <kanji>recreation</kanji>. You ask the woman what she does for fun... for recreation. She says, she goes out and shoots her catapult.
reading_mnemonic: Her favorite thing to shoot at with her catapult for <kanji>recreation</kanji> is <reading>Go</reading>dzilla (ご). Godzilla doesn't notice it, so she can go crazy with the catapult.

meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>measurement</radical> radical and the <kanji>measurement</kanji> kanji are exactly the same.

(Have you ever used one of those triangular rulers? This looks just like one of those, because this is the measurement radical. Just think of all the angles you could measure with this thing!)

"Calculate your enemy's position with accurate <kanji>measurement</kanji>," is more or less what <reading>Sun</reading> (すん) Tzu said, I think. The guy wrote The Art of War, you know. When Sun says measurements are important, you don't question him.

Imagine Mr. Sun measuring distances and rations and whatnot just before going to war — maps, compasses, all kinds of measurement devices piled on his war table. Also, don't forget that in Chinese Sun is pronounced more like "soon."
extra_reading_mnemonic: 寸 refers to a specific measurement of 3.03 centimeters.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>mountain</radical> <radical>wind</radical> coming down from the mountains is very fierce. It is so fierce it's a lot like a <kanji>storm</kanji>. Well, it is a storm, really.

A <kanji>storm</kanji> is nothing to scoff at. If you get hit by the storm and get all wet and nasty and electrocuted, you're bound to get <reading>a rash</reading> (あらし).

The rash comes from being wet and not drying off when you get home. Your skin gets irritated by this moisture.

meaning_mnemonic: If someone puts a <radical>blade</radical> to your <radical>heart</radical>, you're going to have a rough time. They leave it there, for a long time. They aren't going to cut you, but you can't move. You have to <kanji>endure</kanji> the pain and <kanji>conceal</kanji> your discomfort with the situation. To endure something is to conceal how it makes you feel, I guess.
reading_mnemonic:
Learning to <kanji>endure</kanji> and <kanji>conceal</kanji> is all part of your <reading>nin</reading>ja (にん) training. You must learn to stay totally still, without breathing — you have to be able to endure this if you want to conceal yourself.

No one knows better than a ninja how enduring and concealing are closely related. Go ahead, hold your breath and try walking soundlessly around your house, concealing your footsteps. Not easy to endure, is it?
extra_reading_mnemonic: 忍ぶ (しのぶ) - Those who are able <vocabulary>to endure</vocabulary> are those who have had a lot of training. Who has had the most training of anyone? Ninjas. What group are they part of? The <reading>shino</reading>bi (しの).

meaning_mnemonic:
Your <radical>fingers</radical> told you that a <radical>flood</radical> last <radical>evening</radical> would <kanji>draw close</kanji>. There was nothing you could do to stop it, it seemed to be <kanji>be imminent</kanji>, coming in the darkness of the evening.

Think back to last evening, when your fingers twitched and twisted, warning you as the flood started to draw close.
reading_mnemonic: Luckily whenever you sense a flood starting to <kanji>draw close</kanji>, <reading>Satsu</reading>ki (さつ) prepares a raft. Remember Satsuki? Such a talented little girl. She knows that when your fingers twitch and you sat down then that indicates a flood, so it's time to make rafts.

meaning_mnemonic:
You use your <radical>fingers</radical> when you're in <radical>private</radical> to use an <radical>arrow</radical> to <kanji>push open</kanji> things.

You're in private in your own room, no one else is around. Now you wrap your fingers around this big arrow, and you push open your door, your curtains, your windows. It's weird, but you really enjoy this.
reading_mnemonic: Your favorite thing to <kanji>push open</kanji> is your own <reading>eye</reading> (あい). You take the arrow into your fingers and gently push each lid open until you can see. This weirdly makes you see more clearly.

meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>ladle</radical> radical and the <kanji>ladle</kanji> kanji are the same!

(There's a ladle scooping up two drops of liquid. See the handle and the scoop part of the ladle? Imagine ladling some water into your mouth. Mmm.)
reading_mnemonic:
You use a <kanji>ladle</kanji> to distribute soup. But as you're ladling you find something odd floating in the soup. It's... a <reading>toe</reading> (と)! You scream, dropping the ladle and the toe on the ground.

Your mom comes rushing in and smacks you on the head. "Fool!" she says, "This is toe soup, what did you think you'd ladle up?!" Oops.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
一斗缶 - A one <kanji>ladle</kanji> can is a <vocabulary>eighteen-liter container</vocabulary>, which is also a <vocabulary>five-gallon container</vocabulary>. That must be one big ladle!

If you live in Japan you've probably seen these. They're rectangular shaped containers made of metal that are used mostly for industrial purposes, for storing liquids like paint, fuel and chemicals. The 斗 actually refers to an old Japanese measurement, which is roughly equivalent to eighteen liters.

After some consideration, you know who put all those <kanji>limb</kanji>s and <vocabulary>limb</vocabulary>s on the moon. It must've been none other than the moon <reading>shee</reading>p (し)!

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>flowers</radical> <radical>fang</radical> is the bud that comes out of the ground. It's like a little fang, coming from the earth, and it will become a flower someday. This is a little <kanji>sprout</kanji>.

meaning_mnemonic:
No one can <radical>say</radical> what a (weird looking, extra drop) <radical>scooter</radical> weighs in grains of <radical>rice</radical> — it's a <kanji>mystery</kanji>!

meaning_mnemonic:

visually_similar_kanji: 露, 霧, 雲, 雪, 震, 霜, 雰, 電

meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>alligator</radical> is <kanji>considerably</kanji> dangerous. Considerably terrifying too. Considerably [put your scary adjective here]. The radical meaning and the kanji meaning aren't the same, but we'll get through this together.

You feel like a <radical>stone</radical> that’s been <radical>renew</radical>ed. How do renewed stones feel? <kanji>Stiff</kanji>. Very stiff.

Think of a stone being renewed like it is having something like a spa day. Pedicure, manicure, the whole shebang. It’ll come out all stiff and hardened, cause that’s how good stones are.
reading_mnemonic: You remember how you used to cure these <kanji>stiff</kanji> body times: your old friend <reading>こう</reading>いち would just massage them out for you. If only you could ask こういち to give you massages again, but he's too busy for you, now (being emperor and a kanji teacher and all).
extra_reading_mnemonic: 硬い (かたい) - What's the adjective form of <kanji>stiff</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>stiff</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>hard</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>firm</vocabulary>. The reading is the same as a very similar word, 固い (<reading>かたい</reading>). So, if you can use that word to help you to remember, you'll remember the reading of this word in no time as well!

meaning_mnemonic:
Below this <radical>canopy</radical> of <radical>tree</radical>s and <radical>tree</radical>s is a <radical>stone</radical>. Since it's the only stone here, you make sure to <kanji>polish</kanji> it.

It's a single, perfectly round stone under this canopy of trees. It didn't start this way, but thanks to all the polishing you did, it has become nice and smooth.
reading_mnemonic:
You <kanji>polish</kanji> the stone due to your <reading>meager</reading> (みが) lifestyle.

There's only this one stone under these trees, and polishing the stone is the only job here. Still, you don't earn much from it, thus the meager life of polishing your stone.

meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>grain</radical>s you have stored in your <radical>house</radical> reflect on your <kanji>earnings</kanji>. If you earn a lot of money, you have more grains.

Imagine looking at the grains in the houses of people who make vastly different earnings. The poor artist has only a few sacks of grain. The rich samurai has an extra house just for holding his grain. That's how you know he has much higher earnings than the artist.
reading_mnemonic: Another way to check someone's <kanji>earnings</kanji> is to see if they have a <reading>ca</reading>r (か). Would someone who doesn't make a lot of money have a car? No!

meaning_mnemonic:
A (weird looking) <radical>sheep</radical> with <radical>feathers</radical> (and presumably wings, too) is able to <kanji>fly</kanji>.

Imagine the sheep with feathers taking off and flying around. It's an odd sight, but makes sense, kind of.
reading_mnemonic:
Watching that sheep with feathers and wings <kanji>fly</kanji>ing around made you thirsty. You remember that you have a <reading>ca</reading>r <reading>ke</reading>ttle (かけ), so you reach into your car and grab your car kettle to make a special car-kettle brew.

Imagine yourself enjoying the cozy car-kettle brew, while admiring the unusual sight of the sheep with feathers and wings flying through the sky. This is just shear bliss!

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>moon</radical> <radical>table</radical> is a table that's made entirely of <kanji>skin</kanji>. You thought the table was made of moon, with all those pores and such, but when you look more closely, you realize it's skin. Disgusting, porous, skin.
reading_mnemonic: But, when you go to touch this "moon table" made of <kanji>skin</kanji>, you realize that it's <reading>harder</reading> (はだ) than you expected. Touch it and feel the "moon table." You'd think skin would be softer, but it's pretty hard. Much harder than you expected.

meaning_mnemonic: If you've been to the <radical>moon</radical> in the <radical>past</radical>, you had to get the special <radical>stamp</radical> on your <kanji>leg</kanji>. This leg stamp not only proved you went, but lets everyone around you know you've been to the moon before!
reading_mnemonic: You've only met one other person with the same mark on their <kanji>leg</kanji> and it was <reading>Kyaku</reading> (きゃく) the customer. Kyaku visits many places all over the world, so it only makes sense that they've also been off-world too. Picture Kyaku lifting up their pant leg and showing you all the stamps from all the different places they've been.
extra_reading_mnemonic: Wondering how 脚 and 足 differ? You might remember 足 is mostly for feet but can sometimes refer to legs. 脚 refers to the whole <vocabulary>leg</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>lower limb</vocabulary> (often including the foot). Basically, go with 足 for feet and 脚 for legs! The reading (<reading>あし</reading>) is the same as 足!

meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>boat</radical> radical and the <kanji>boat</kanji> kanji are the same!

(This looks like a boat coming toward you in the water. See the sail billowing on top and the reflection on the water? Yep, that's a boat. The boatiest boat that ever boated.)
reading_mnemonic:
The reading is the same reading that you learned with the vocabulary 船 (<reading>ふね</reading>). Since 船 and 舟 both mean "boat", this reading should be pretty easy to remember! 

Note that this word 舟 isn't usually used by itself (that would be 船). It's usually attached to things that are boat-related.
extra_reading_mnemonic: When you're riding a <kanji>boat</kanji>, you might get wet, so make sure to pack an extra pair of <reading>shoes</reading> (しゅう).

meaning_mnemonic:
When you leave <radical>flowers</radical> in your <radical>mouth</radical> with<radical>grain</radical>s for long enough, they'll turn into flowers of <kanji>bacteria</kanji>. These aren't the nice, pretty flowers you'd give your mom on Mother's Day. These are little bacteria flowers that are taking over your mouth. That's a lot of nasty bacteria! Maybe brush your teeth next time.

~~~ When you leave <radical>grain</radical>s in your <radical>mouth</radical> for long enough, they'll turn into <radical>flowers</radical> of <kanji>bacteria</kanji>.
reading_mnemonic:
There is a lot of this <kanji>bacteria</kanji> in the <reading>Kin</reading>g (きん) of England's mouth. He eats a lot of grains, and he won't let anyone touch his mouth to clean it, but he refuses to do things himself... so it's absolutely chock full of bacteria.

Picture the King's mouth up close. Look at all the bacteria squiggling around and through his teeth and gums. Bleh! Barf!

meaning_mnemonic:
If your <radical>outfit</radical> is just a piece of <radical>fruit</radical>, then you are <kanji>naked</kanji>.

You're like one of those nudes in a Renaissance painting, strategically covering yourself with a bunch of grapes or a well-placed apple or something.
reading_mnemonic: You know who else is often <kanji>naked</kanji>? The ancient Egyptian god <reading>Ra</reading> (ら). Well, half-naked at least. Egypt is a hot country, so you can't really blame Ra for wanting to strip down.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 裸 (はだか) - You are <kanji>naked</kanji> now (with Ra). You used to wear a car costume, but you don't have it anymore (and you're not wearing it). You <reading>had a ca</reading>r (はだか), but now you don't have a car. That's what you'll explain when someone asks you why you're naked.

meaning_mnemonic: I'm putting all my <radical>shellfish</radical> on <radical>someone</radical>, hoping they'll win the race! This is a <kanji>gamble</kanji> and you're gambling. Remember, shellfish used to be used as money. So if you're betting shellfish on someone, you're gambling.
reading_mnemonic:
If you win this <kanji>gamble</kanji> you'll have enough shellfish to buy a brand new <reading>ca</reading>r (か)!

If you go to any of those fancy (and not so fancy) gamble-places, they always have a car sitting in the middle of the room. Usually rotating, really slowly, to make you want it more, making you gamble more.

meaning_mnemonic: Something made of <radical>gold</radical> <radical>stand</radical>s in a <radical>village</radical>. It's a <kanji>bell</kanji>!  The village bell, standing tall and proud and shiny in the village for everyone to see and hear.
reading_mnemonic:
The <kanji>bell</kanji> rings whenever the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう) arrives in the village. Its ringing echoes throughout the entire village so everyone knows they have to come out and pay their respects.

The Shougun bell even sounds like it's warning you that the Shougun has arrived. It makes a loud, low shooooouu shooou sound.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 鐘 (かね) usually refers to larger, open-ended <vocabulary>bell</vocabulary>s of the sort you might find in a church's bell tower or a Buddhist temple. Seeing the <vocabulary>bell</vocabulary>, you decide you need to ring it. You take your <reading>cane</reading> (かね) and hit the bell as hard as you can, making it chime.

meaning_mnemonic: This <radical>building</radical> <radical>now</radical> has a <radical>cloud</radical> over it, creating <kanji>shade</kanji>. Ahh, shade is so nice and cool.
reading_mnemonic:
The building that's getting this nice <kanji>shade</kanji> is the <reading>inn</reading> (いん) you're staying at.

Picture an inn with a cloud right above it right now. Look at the cloud-shaped shade keeping everyone visiting the inn cool and sunburn-free.
extra_reading_mnemonic: The <vocabulary>shade</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>shadow</vocabulary> is similar to Shadow 影 (<reading>かげ</reading>).

meaning_mnemonic: Coming down with the <radical>rain</radical> is <radical>two</radical> <radical>spikes</radical>. They go right through two <kanji>ghost</kanji>s. The ghosts are pinned to the ground by the spikes, unable to move.
reading_mnemonic:
You come across the <kanji>ghost</kanji>s, who are stabbed into the ground. "Please," they beg. "Please use that <reading>ray</reading> (れい) gun that's in that <reading>row</reading> (りょう) boat and end our suffering."

A ray gun, coincidentally, is the only thing that can kill a ghost, and there it lays. You'll have to be the one to pull the trigger of the ray gun. Do you pick up the ray gun out of the row boat to destroy the ghosts?

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>spoon</radical> to measure/weigh a <radical>geoduck</radical> is a very <kanji>approximate</kanji> measurement/weight. Geoducks are big, spoons are small. Still, we'll get the approximation going, right?
reading_mnemonic: Maybe this is too much geoduck, even if we're going for an <kanji>approximate</kanji>. So, you take the <reading>core</reading> (ころ) of the geoduck and measure that instead.
extra_reading_mnemonic: ころ tends to get rendaku'd to <reading>ごろ</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>cloud</radical> floating above a <radical>demon</radical> has its <kanji>soul</kanji> in it. If you can manage to get through to the demon, to make it see that it doesn't have to be evil, it might remember who it is and return to the <kanji>spirit</kanji> it once was.
reading_mnemonic:
You shout out and beg its <kanji>soul</kanji> for help until, finally, you see the cloud take the shape of a <reading>con</reading>dor (こん). Aha! "You were a condor before you became a demon! Remember who you are and turn back!"

POOF! Now there's a condor spirit floating in front of you, crying. "Thank you, human. You've saved my soul!" it says, and float/flies off and disappears.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 魂 (たましい) - Look inside your <kanji>soul</kanji>. You see all the bits and bobs that make up your <vocabulary>soul</vocabulary> rolling around and around, being pushed by the Katamari <reading>Tamashii</reading> (たましい). He keeps your soul nice and big and safe!

meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>leader</radical> has a (without a slide) <radical>life</radical> and <radical>kick</radical>s at the <kanji>straw sack</kanji> you are holding. This leader is taking his frustrations out on this sack.

See this leader's kick coming at your straw sack. Hear the leader yelling as he aims his kick at your straw sack. Hiyahhh! Also keep in mind that the life radical is missing the little drop/slide thing on the side. It's missing that because your life is lousy and sad.
reading_mnemonic: You manage to get your <kanji>straw sack</kanji> out of the way as you shout "<reading>Heyo</reading> (ひょう)! Look, you missed! Heyo!" Unfortunately your leader's friend was standing behind you and he kicks your sack as you move it out of the way. "Heyo!" he shouts, mockingly.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 俵 (たわら) - A bunch of <vocabulary>straw sack</vocabulary>s or <vocabulary>straw bag</vocabulary>s are stacked upon each other to make a tower (たわら). Imagine walking into this sack tower and wondering how it's all held together. Such poor architecture.

meaning_mnemonic: I have <radical>five</radical> things in my <radical>mouth</radical> and <kanji>I</kanji> need them all for <kanji>me</kanji>. I own these five things, and I keep them in my mouth so people like you cannot take them from me.
reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Me</kanji>, personally, <kanji>I</kanji> am quite thirsty so I ask for some “<reading>waga</reading>” (わが). I have five things in my mouth, so it is hard for me to pronounce the word “water”. So it sounds like “waga” when I ask for it. “Coulg I pweash hab sum waga?! I deed waga!!”

meaning_mnemonic: You use <radical>black</radical> <radical>dirt</radical> to make <kanji>black ink</kanji>. That's what you use to write in black! The dirt you're using to make black ink is really, really black. Like the kind you find around volcanoes or something.
reading_mnemonic: Be careful that you don't spill <kanji>black ink</kanji> on anyone or anything. If you do, you have to own it. Imagine spilling black ink on someone, and when they confront you, you yell, "Yeah I got black ink on you, so <reading>sue me</reading> (すみ)!" Imagine yelling "SUE ME!" at someone's face, which is covered in the black ink you spilled there.

visually_similar_kanji: 礼, 札, 乱, 乳
meaning_mnemonic:
You see a <radical>child</radical> with an <radical>umbrella</radical> in front of you. Suddenly, they fall straight down into a <kanji>cavity</kanji> in the road. It's a big <kanji>hole</kanji>!

You run over to where the child fell. They are just fine! Because they had an umbrella, they were able to float to the bottom.
reading_mnemonic: "Into my <kanji>cavity</kanji> you go!" yells a voice. It is <reading>こう</reading>いち. "You will stay in that cavity or hole until you worship me!"

radical_characters: 宀, 心, 罒, 丁
meaning_mnemonic:
On the <radical>roof</radical> is your <radical>heart</radical>. OR! In a <radical>net</radical> in the <radical>street</radical>. Which would you <kanji>rather</kanji>?

Would you rather have your heart up on the roof, close to falling but out of the way of people. Or would you rather have your heart in a net, which people can't steal from, but is in the way of cars.
reading_mnemonic:
As you try to decide which you'd <kanji>rather</kanji> have, your <reading>neigh</reading>bors (ねい) come out and grab the heart out of your hands.

"I'd rather you didn't have that!" you shout as your neighbors run through the neighborhood to their own house. You'd rather this wasn't happening! You'd rather your neighbors let you make your own choice!!
extra_reading_mnemonic: 寧ろ (むしろ) - This is the same as the kanji, <kanji>rather</kanji>. Can also mean <vocabulary>better</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>instead</vocabulary>. Just think: <vocabulary>rather</vocabulary> than a <reading>bug</reading> (むし), how about an animal?

meaning_mnemonic:
You need to bring <radical>charcoal</radical> under this <radical>roof</radical> to heat the <kanji>dormitory</kanji>. You live in this dormitory with a bunch of other kids, and you all have to take turns bringing in the charcoal from outside to heat it.

Imagine looking at a dormitory chore wheel and seeing it's your turn to carry in the charcoal this week. Bleh!
reading_mnemonic:
The <kanji>dormitory</kanji> is on an island, so when you go out to get the charcoal you have to take a <reading>row</reading> (りょう) boat. You row and row and row until you reach the shed with all the charcoal. Then you row and row and row it back to the dormitory.

The dormitory row boat leaks a little too, so by the time you get back you really need to light the charcoal and heat up!

meaning_mnemonic: You <radical>stand</radical> on a <radical>forehead</radical> with a <radical>towel</radical> because you're the <kanji>sovereign</kanji>. As a sovereign, you're too important to be getting your shoes dirty. Everywhere you go, you're standing on foreheads with a towel — that's how people know you're the sovereign.
reading_mnemonic:
And it's not just any towel you stand on. To show that you're the <kanji>sovereign</kanji>, it has the symbol of a <reading>ta</reading>ter (てい) tot on it. The mighty, sovereign tater tot! That's how everyone knows it belongs to the sovereign.

On top of being the sovereign of breakfast foods, the tater also symbolizes all the qualities of a good sovereign: humble and accessible; firm on the outside, but with a soft and warm heart; and always providing nourishment to the people… or something.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 帝 (みかど) is a classical term for the emperor in Japan. It's found in works of classical literature, historical novels, or period dramas that are set in feudal Japan. In modern Japanese, the Japanese emperor is called 天皇. To remember the reading, think about how the <vocabulary>Japanese Emperor</vocabulary>, can always pull out his "<reading>me card</reading>" (みかど) when he's in trouble. It's kind of like how a "trump card" is the one that's above all the others, but with the emperor he's always up there, so it's a "me card" to him. And who's gonna argue with the emperor? Not me.

meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Poop</radical> <radical>Poop</radical> <radical>Mountain</radical> is covered in poop because it is such a <kanji>secluded</kanji> place. A secluded place has no toilets, so you just poop right on the mountain.
reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>secluded</kanji> Poop Poop Mountain is a favorite of <reading>you</reading>ths (ゆう). They go there to get away from their phones to get in touch with nature again. Eww, those are some nasty youths with no self-awareness or self-control.

meaning_mnemonic:
You're standing under a <radical>canopy</radical> when you see something strange sticking out of the <radical>dirt</radical>. You pull it, but it won't budge. You pull harder and harder until the dirt starts rumbling and a giant <kanji>manor</kanji> starts rising out of the ground with you on top!

Picture yourself on top of this manor that rose out of the ground. The canopy is still above you and it seems to be attached to the roof.
reading_mnemonic: The beautiful <kanji>manor</kanji> begins to shake and the <reading>shou</reading>gun (しょう) bursts out of the front door. "WHO HAS UNEARTHED MY SECRET MANOR?!" he screams.

visually_similar_kanji: 暫, 析, 折, 祈, 新
meaning_mnemonic: You use your <radical>car</radical> and an <radical>axe</radical> to <kanji>slice</kanji> down a pedestrian. This innocent guy is just walking along the road when you drive up to him in your car and axe him to death with your axe. You’re all like, VROOM! AXE! Now this guy is dead because you sliced him down in cold blood.
reading_mnemonic: You were driving around in <reading>Zan</reading>zibar (ざん) when you <kanji>slice</kanji>d down this man. Luckily, Zanzibar has no laws at all, so you won’t get arrested for slicing down this guy with your axe.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 斬る (きる) - The kanji itself means <kanji>slice</kanji> and the verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to cut down</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to slice off</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to lop off</vocabulary>. This word mainly refers to cutting people with a sword, if you haven't figured it out yet. The reading is the same as 切る (<reading>きる</reading>), which means "to cut." Similar meaning, same reading.

meaning_mnemonic:
With the <radical>power</radical> of your <radical>mouth</radical> you command a <radical>tree</radical> to become a <kanji>shelf</kanji>. Most of the time one would have to use their hands and tools to turn a tree into a shelf, but you are capable of turning a tree into a shelf by using the power of your mouth.

Imagine using your mouth to turn a tree into a shelf. Yell at this tree and keep yelling at it until you see it become a shelf.
reading_mnemonic:
Once you turn the tree into a <kanji>shelf</kanji> you put the shelf in your <reading>ca</reading>r (か) and sell it at a local pawn shop. You keep doing this over and over again until you are rich. You command the trees to turn into shelves and then you take the shelves in your car to sell them. Easy money.

Imagine transporting the shelves in your car. Over and over. Back and forth in your car. Vroom vroom.

visually_similar_kanji: 練, 陣, 錬, 陳
meaning_mnemonic:
There’s a <radical>tree</radical> in the <radical>east</radical> that looks like a <kanji>building</kanji>. The tree is tall and straight and doesn't have any leaves or branches. It's basically a big wooden building.

Look at this big tree building over in the east. Imagine actually using it as a building and moving in. And why not? It's free real estate.
reading_mnemonic:
That <kanji>building</kanji> happens to be in the center of <reading>とう</reading>きょう. If you need to find east (which is where とうきょう is), you just look for the building.

Imagine looking down on とうきょう from the top floor of this magnificent building you've just moved into.

meaning_mnemonic:
This <radical>tree</radical> is very <radical>odd</radical>, to say the least. The shape is all crazy, like a lightning bolt stuck into the ground, or something. Oh wait, look at this. I can sit on it really nicely. It's just like a <kanji>chair</kanji>!

Imagine this odd tree <kanji>chair</kanji> being the most comfortable chair you've ever sat on. It's shaped perfectly for you, and the moss makes it soft. Wow, what a chair.
reading_mnemonic: But, this odd tree <kanji>chair</kanji> is also home to an <reading>ea</reading>gle (い). It swoops down upon you as you sit down, sitting on the chair with you.

meaning_mnemonic: You have to <radical>stop</radical> keeping <radical>canine</radical>s when you and they are <radical>small</radical> since you need to be at a certain number of <kanji>years old</kanji>. You'll be hitting that age requirement this <kanji>year</kanji>, which means your <kanji>time</kanji> with your small canine will keep continuing.
reading_mnemonic: Remember the vocab word 〜才 which also meant "<kanji>years old</kanji>"? Well, this has the same reading: <reading>さい</reading>.
extra_reading_mnemonic: When you increase your number of <kanji>years old</kanji>, you celebrate by waving your <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい) around. Another year gone, cut! A new year awaits.

visually_similar_kanji: 飽, 胞, 抱, 包, 砲
meaning_mnemonic:
If a <radical>tsunami</radical> <radical>wrap</radical>s around itself, the resulting wave will create a lot of <kanji>bubbles</kanji>. You know how tsunamis wrap around once gravity kicks in, right? Well when that wave crashes, a whole lot of bubbles are created.

Picture the bubbles bursting out of the wrapped up tsunami as it crashes down. The air that the tsunami sucked in while it was wrapping up come out as bubbles big and small.
reading_mnemonic: One of the biggest <kanji>bubbles</kanji> heads straight for your <reading>ho</reading>me (ほう), engulfs it, and picks it up into the air! Watch as you in your home, now trapped in a bubble, float away into the sky.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
It's a <vocabulary>bubble</vocabulary>!

Huh? <reading>A Wha---</reading>? (あわ)

A BUBBLE.

A WHA???

meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>animal</radical> that <radical>kick</radical>s <radical>dirt</radical> into people's <radical>mouth</radical>s is a <kanji>monkey</kanji>. (An animal that puts dirt in peoples' mouth by kicking it is a monkey). Monkeys are naughty little things. You should be happy it was just dirt it kicked into your mouth, and not something worse.
reading_mnemonic: You spit the dirt out of your mouth and look back at the <kanji>monkey</kanji> to see that it's <reading>salu</reading>ting (さる) you. Is... is it mocking you?

meaning_mnemonic:
When you get <radical>sick</radical> you always eat a <radical>hot pepper</radical>. It's a <kanji>habit</kanji> you've picked up and you can't seem to shake it. One sniffle, one cough, and before you know it, you're eating a hot pepper or two.

Imagine if you had a habit of eating hot peppers whenever you thought you might be getting sick. To be fair, it flushes out your sinuses and tastes good, so it's not the worst habit you could have.
reading_mnemonic:
Everyone you know has a different <kanji>habit</kanji> when they get sick. Instead, they eat <reading>cous</reading>cous (くせ). But you think couscous is gross. It's bland and does nothing for your stuffy noses and scratchy throats. I wonder how you can convince them to replace their habit with your own.

Unfortunately, now you've gotten into the habit of telling everyone what to do when they get sick. "Yeah, yeah, eat a hot pepper, we know. But couscous is better," they say before you can speak. To each their own, I suppose.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 癖 (くせ) - The kanji itself means <kanji>habit</kanji> but it usually refers to a <vocabulary>bad habit</vocabulary>, so try to remember that meaning if you could.

other_meanings: Ancestral Festival, Bon, Obon, Festival Of The Dead, Obon Festival, Lantern Festival, Ancestry Festival, Bon Festival
meaning_mnemonic:
You put <radical>part</radical> of your food on a <radical>plate</radical>, then put that on a <kanji>tray</kanji> to keep it safe. This tray is an offering for the <kanji>ancestral festival</kanji>, where your ancestors' spirits visit you to check in and share some of that food you're offering on a tray.

Imagine preparing this tray, just before your ancestors arrive in friendly ghost form to share part of your meal with you. They only come once a year, so make sure it's a nice tray, okay?
reading_mnemonic:
The plate you put on the <kanji>tray</kanji> for the <kanji>ancestral festival</kanji> is made of <reading>bone</reading> (ぼん). Bone china, that is. How fancy… And appropriate, considering bone china is made from actual bone.

Tap the bone china plate with your knuckle bone. Hear the pleasant clink it makes as you set it on the tray.

meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>eye</radical> gets kicked with a <radical>cleat</radical> that came careening toward your <radical>forehead</radical> when it popped off someone doing a <radical>dance</radical>, and you <kanji>blink</kanji>. Well, of course you blink, you can't control that. And when a cleat come hurtling toward your eye it blinks automatically.
reading_mnemonic: You <kanji>blink</kanji> and blink and <reading>soon</reading> (しゅん) there are tears coming out of them too. You try to blink them away but it's not working. extra_reading_mnemonic:
妃 (きさき) - The kanji and the vocabulary are exactly the same, so this means <vocabulary>royal consort</vocabulary>. Depending on who she's married to, she could be a <vocabulary>queen</vocabulary>, a <vocabulary>princess</vocabulary>, or even an <vocabulary>empress</vocabulary>. How do you know someone is a <vocabulary>royal consort</vocabulary>? Because they <reading>kiss a ki</reading>ng (きさき). If you kiss a king, maybe you can be a royal consort too!

妃 can overlap in meaning with 后, but 后 is reserved for the highest-ranking consort, like an empress or queen, while 妃 is a more general word which includes lower-ranking consorts and the wives of other royal family members. In modern Japanese, the kana version きさき often appears in fairytale-style stories with kings and queens. But it's good to know both kanji, especially if you're reading anything historical.
