reading_mnemonic: The world has united against the moon. "We have <kanji>agreement</kanji>," the world's leaders all say. "We will work together to stop the moon, and we have <kanji>agreement</kanji> on who we will follow, Emperor <reading>こう</reading>いち.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
肯く (うなずく) (うなづく) - If you want to show your <kanji>agreement</kanji> with someone you need <vocabulary>to nod</vocabulary> at them so they know. After the world agreement to stop the moon, you seem <vocabulary>to nod</vocabulary> your head a lot. This is because you want to go to the <reading>una</reading>gi <reading>zoo</reading> (うなず). Unagi zoos are really rare and hard to get into. So while you're there, keep nodding to everyone because you're so honored to be there!

肯く also has two readings. うなずく is the standard, but うなづく is more and more acceptable these days too. Luckily they sound pretty similar (if not the same), so they should be easy to remember!

meaning_mnemonic:
You ate the <radical>moon</radical> with a <radical>spoon</radical>, and then the <radical>sun</radical> too, but man were they high in <kanji>fat</kanji>! In fact, you wanted to eat them with chopsticks, but they were so greasy with fat that the spoon was your only option.

Not only did you eat two really important celestial bodies, but their high fat content made them way less healthy than you expected.
reading_mnemonic:
Unbeknownst to you, the moon and sun contained as much <kanji>fat</kanji> as an entire adult <reading>shee</reading>p (し)! Why didn't you check the nutrition facts first???

If you had known you were going to get a whole sheep's worth of fat, you would have just eaten a big platter of mutton chops instead of dooming the entire solar system by eating the moon and sun.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 脂身 (あぶらみ) - The <kanji>fat</kanji> on an animal's <kanji>body</kanji> is called <vocabulary>fatty meat</vocabulary>. Some people really like to eat it and others really like to hate it. Mmm, all that <vocabulary>fatty meat</vocabulary>. Think about fatty meat on your own body. If you have a lot of fatty meat, then you need a way to support said fatty meat. To do that, you would use <reading>a bra</reading> (あぶら).

meaning_mnemonic:
If you look in a <radical>tiger</radical>'s <radical>stomach</radical> you'll find a bunch of <kanji>skin</kanji>. It's really gross but what else did you think you'd find? Everyone knows tigers can't digest the skin of the things it eats.

Imagine yourself opening a tigers mouth and looking all the way down into its stomach and seeing a bunch of skin. Eww.
reading_mnemonic:
The only person who would try to take <kanji>skin</kanji> from a tiger's stomach is a <reading>foo</reading>l (ふ). You'll probably get your head bitten off looking for skin that way.

Imagine a fool trying to pull skin out of a tiger's stomach. You can imagine them getting their skin added to the pile too if you want.

meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Flowers</radical> that grow in a <radical>rice paddy</radical> only live to be <kanji>seedling</kanji>s. Once they sprout, they're plucked away to make room for more rice. Poor little seedlings.
reading_mnemonic:
The <kanji>seedling</kanji>s try their best to blend in by referring to themselves as <reading>myou</reading> (みょう), you know, me and you combined. That's myou.

Listen to the little seedlings say myou over and over. Too bad the farmers can tell they aren't rice plants.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 苗 (なえ) - The best time to plant <vocabulary>seedling</vocabulary>s is at <reading>nigh</reading>t (なえ). If you plant them at night they'll sleep through the whole transplanting process and they'll wake up happy and ready to grow.

meaning_mnemonic: You put <radical>flowers</radical> on your <radical>car</radical> and your <radical>scooter</radical>. The flowers you put on them are <kanji>lotus</kanji> flowers.
reading_mnemonic: You're putting a <kanji>lotus</kanji> on both your scooter and car because they are <reading>ren</reading>tals (れん). You always put a lotus on top of your rental cars and scooters. It just makes those boring, ugly rental cars and scooters so much prettier!
extra_reading_mnemonic: 蓮 (はす) - A <kanji>lotus</kanji> is, well, a <vocabulary>lotus</vocabulary>. In Buddhist scripture, though, it's often a <vocabulary>sacred lotus</vocabulary>. If you spot one growing in a random pond somewhere, it's probably the former, but if it looks all ethereal and there's a Buddha sitting on it, it's probably the latter, so use your judgment!  Whenever you see a <vocabulary>lotus</vocabulary>, you call your trusty pet <reading>hus</reading>ky (はす). Lotuses grow out in the middle of ponds, but you've trained your husky to swim out and get them. Picture your husky swimming back with a lotus in its mouth, panting happily: "hus, hus, hus!" Your husky is just the goodest boy.

meaning_mnemonic:
What <radical>outfit</radical> do you wear when cutting down <radical>tree</radical>s and <radical>tree</radical>s with a <radical>jackhammer</radical>? A <kanji>collar</kanji>. Yup, just a collar… plus some shirt cuffs and slacks, of course. You know, the classic Chippendales look? 

This collar is what you always wear when you do your "hot lumberjack" act. If you were seriously trying to cut down trees, you wouldn't be using a jackhammer, after all.
reading_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>collar</kanji> has "<reading>Eri</reading>c" (えり) emblazoned on it in cursive letters, because this is the stage name you use when you do your lumberjack act. Eric's not your real name, of course — you just think it sounds hunky and looks good on a collar.

Imagine standing there in your collar, jackhammering trees as all your swooning fans scream "Eric! Eriiiic! We love you!" from the audience.

meaning_mnemonic: You try to put your <radical>toe</radical> inside a <radical>shellfish</radical>, but it just won't open. That's because this shellfish has sworn an oath of <kanji>chastity</kanji>. "No, I won't open up until I meet the toe I will marry," it says to you.
reading_mnemonic:
"<kanji>Chastity</kanji> is really important to me," the shellfish says. "But, maybe if you give me a <reading>ta</reading>ter (てい) tot, I'll change my mind."

You give the shellfish a tater tot, and it breaks its vow of chastity, opening up for your toe. You look the other way, but you can hear the sounds of passion below. Whoa.

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>car</radical> that's <radical>lack</radical>ing is really <kanji>soft</kanji>. Cars need to be hard so that things like bugs and other cars wont hurt the people inside when you hit them. But if your car is lacking the hardness it needs, you'll have a really soft, useless car.
reading_mnemonic:
This car is probably so <kanji>soft</kanji> because it's made entirely of <reading>naan</reading> (なん). Naan may be delicious, but it makes a really crappy car. No wonder it was so soft (and yummy).

Picture trying to drive this soft naan car. It probably just sinks into the ground and then gets eaten by wild animals (and me).
extra_reading_mnemonic: 軟らかい (やわらかい) - While 柔らかい describes a pleasant, gentle softness or graceful flexibility, 軟らかい refers to <vocabulary>soft</vocabulary>ness or pliability as an objective physical property. So, for example, 柔らかいお肉 is the delicious, tender steak you have at a fancy restaurant, while 軟らかいお肉 simply describes the only kind of meat your toothless granny can eat. Likewise, a graceful gymnast or ballerina has a 柔らかい体, while your friend who can fit himself inside a suitcase — well, he has an objectively 軟らかい体. Since this is an alternate version of 柔らかい (<reading>やわらかい</reading>), it has the same reading too. If you remember that, you can remember this word's reading.

visually_similar_kanji: 抵, 低, 底, 紙
meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>clan</radical> is on the <radical>ground</radical> next to a <radical>building</radical>, which is your new <kanji>residence</kanji>. You're all together in your new home!
reading_mnemonic:
Your new <kanji>residence</kanji> is complete! You step closer and the smell of <reading>ta</reading>ter (てい) tots hits your nose. Someone is making you tater tots in your new residence. Wait, no they aren't. Your residence is MADE of tater tots! Yum! 

Now that you live in a tater tot residence, whenever you're hungry, you just lean over to the wall and munch.

visually_similar_kanji: 効, 較, 絞, 校
meaning_mnemonic: If you <radical>mix</radical> a bunch of <radical>building</radical>s together, you have yourself a <kanji>suburb</kanji>. Isn't that all a suburb is? Just a mix of a variety of buildings in one area?
reading_mnemonic: "<kanji>Suburb</kanji>s are what we need!" says Emperor <reading>こう</reading>いち. "That suburb life will encourage more people to study kanji," Emperor こういち continues.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>buddy</radical> <radical>building</radical> is in your <kanji>county</kanji>. It is in your county, so you're able to hang out a lot with your buddy building.
reading_mnemonic: Your <kanji>county</kanji> is everything you can reach when shooting a <reading>gun</reading> (ぐん). If the bullet can reach a building you know, it's a buddy building in your county.

meaning_mnemonic: If you use a <radical>sickle</radical> to kill a <radical>shrimp</radical> you'll need a really good <kanji>explanation</kanji> for yourself. What did that shrimp do to you? Why use a sickle? Well? What's your explanation?
reading_mnemonic: In your <kanji>explanation</kanji> you blame everything on <reading>Shaq</reading> (しゃく). He told you to do it! It's all Shaq's fault, you explain. This is payback for Shaq dunking on you during a basketball scrimmage.

meaning_mnemonic:
So my <radical>building</radical> has a big <radical>splinter</radical>, right in the <kanji>corner</kanji>. So what?

Imagine a huge splinter coming out of the corner of the building. It's in a really dangerous spot, but the owner doesn't seem so worried about it.
reading_mnemonic: That <kanji>corner</kanji> is dangerous, but what are you going to do, <reading>sue me</reading> (すみ)? Actually, please don't sue me. I'll fix the splinter coming out of the corner of my building.

other_meanings: Counter For Ships, Ships, Counter For Vessels, Vessel Counter, Vessels, Fleets, Fleet Counter, Counter For Fleets, Number Of Ships, Number Of Vessels, Number Of Fleets
meaning_mnemonic:
A <radical>turkey</radical> sitting on a <radical>stool</radical> is something every ship has in its crow's nest. That's why the universal <kanji>ship counter</kanji> is a turkey on a stool. Not a crow.

Picture yourself counting ships by pointing your finger from one turkey propped up on a stool to the next. You'll be the best ship counter in the world at this rate!
reading_mnemonic: Once you become the best <kanji>ship counter</kanji> in the world everyone will think you are super <reading>sexy</reading> (せき)! Nothing is sexier than being able to count, and counting ships is the sexiest thing you can count.

meaning_mnemonic:
Take the <radical>street</radical> all the way to that <radical>geoduck</radical>, way up there. When you reach it, you will have made it to the <kanji>summit</kanji>. You <kanji>humbly</kanji> present the road to the geoduck and bow before it.

There is a giant geoduck at the summit of the mountain, and the street will lead you right there. Imagine the grueling climb up the mountain to the summit. Feel it in your legs, and keep looking at that tall, tall geoduck. Now imagine kneeling those same aching legs humbly to the street below the geoduck.
reading_mnemonic:
You are at the top, the <kanji>summit</kanji> of everything! You <kanji>humbly</kanji> survey your surroundings from the top of the geoduck, only to see someone on the street, running toward you. It is Mrs. <reading>Chou</reading> (ちょう), and she looks angry.

Anytime you use the street, you're in Mrs. Chou's territory. Remember, wherever there's a street (radical), Mrs. Chou is not far behind.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 頂く (いただく) - If you <kanji>humbly</kanji> do something you are going <vocabulary>to humbly receive</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to humbly accept</vocabulary>, or eat or drink it. Basically you're humbly doing a lot of things. And you can use this word for all of them! You technically already know this reading! You know how people say いただきます? Well that's the same as this! You're humbly receiving your meal. So <vocabulary>to humbly receive</vocabulary> is <reading>いただ</reading>く!

kunyomi: の, なんじ, すなわ
meaning_mnemonic:
What do <radical>stairs</radical> do? They take you <kanji>from</kanji> where you were, to somewhere else. They're a way to get <kanji>from</kanji> place to place. 

Picture yourself climbing stairs, picture going from room to room. From place to place. From wherever you were to wherever you want to be.

(This radical looks like a little flight of stairs, don't you think? Also note it's being held up by a pillar or beam or something on the left side. After all, you don't want your stairs collapsing as you walk up them.)
reading_mnemonic:
If you're going <kanji>from</kanji> place to place, make sure you have some <reading>no</reading>ri (の) seaweed on you, in case you get hungry. Nori is a great source of energy.

Imagine yourself going from one place to another with your pockets stuffed full of nori. The smell is starting to get overwhelming. It's making you really hungry (or nauseous, depending on how you feel about nori!).

meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>leader</radical> puts their <radical>hat</radical> on the <radical>ground</radical> next to a <radical>bookshelf</radical>. This is a test in <kanji>ethics</kanji>. People hang around the bookshelf, and the leader wants to see if anyone will steal the hat or not. That's why its a test of ethics.
reading_mnemonic: To test your <kanji>ethics</kanji> even more, the leader puts down a <reading>rin</reading>g (りん) as well. Now we'll really see how everyone's ethics are. Will they turn in the expensive ring to the lost and found? Will they ignore it? Will they steal it?

meaning_mnemonic:
The <radical>leader</radical> of the <radical>library</radical> thinks that all the books in their library are better than everyone else's books. He's a very <kanji>biased</kanji> person. If he wasn't the leader of that specific library he'd probably feel differently.

Imagine showing the leader your favorite book. "That's not a book in MY library," he says, and throws it in the trash. That's so biased! He didn't even give it a shot!
reading_mnemonic: You decide to give in to his <kanji>biased</kanji> recommendations and look at what he has in his library. It doesn't take long until you realize that these books are all about <reading>hen</reading>s (へん) and hen care. This guy is so biased about his favorite books that he only filled his library with what HE wants to read. And apparently that thing is taking care of hens... weird.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 偏る (かたよる) - The kanji itself means <kanji>biased</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to be biased</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be prejudiced</vocabulary>. You meet someone who claims <vocabulary>to be biased</vocabulary> about everything. You ask them why and they say, "I'm a <reading>cutter, yo</reading> (かたよ)! I cut everything in half and only like one of 'em. But I guess if you wanna call that biased go ahead, man." Huh, okay.

meaning_mnemonic:
I hope all you're doing in the <radical>bathtub</radical> is taking a <kanji>bath</kanji>. I mean, you can do other things if you want I guess. But bathtubs were made just for baths!

(See the dude sitting inside the box? His head is sticking out the top. That's a bathtub he's sitting in.)
reading_mnemonic: When do you miss taking a <kanji>bath</kanji> the most? When you're on the <reading>ro</reading>ad (ろ). Traveling is fun and all, but when you're stuck in a car, traveling down a dirt road for days, all you want to do is take a nice long bath.

meaning_mnemonic:
Beside your <radical>mouth</radical> is an evil <radical>spider</radical> that tries to <kanji>instigate</kanji> you into saying bad things and starting a riot. It's like the little silken puppet master of your mouth or something. Don't let it instigate you!

Imagine this spider controlling your mouth with its web, making you say things you wouldn't dare think of. "Free healthcare for all!" "Pineapple is a legitimate pizza topping!" Man, you gotta stop letting that spider instigate you into saying weird stuff.

Instigate means "to initiate, provoke, or urge someone to take a specific action".
reading_mnemonic: You want the spider to stop <kanji>instigate</kanji>-ing you into saying bad things and starting riots. So you pick up a <reading>saw</reading> (さ) and start cutting off the silken threads that are controlling your mouth. If this spider's web is strong enough to control your mouth, you will most likely need a saw to cut it off, right?

radical_characters: 口, 十, 艹, 貝
meaning_mnemonic:
From your <radical>mouth</radical> comes a <radical>cross</radical>, some <radical>flowers</radical>, and <radical>shellfish</radical>. It all <kanji>erupt</kanji>s from your mouth!

Imagine these three things coming out of your mouth not one at a time, but all together like an eruption.
reading_mnemonic:
When do inanimate objects <kanji>erupt</kanji> from your mouth? Mostly when you're having <reading>fun</reading> (ふん). It's really inconvenient that things erupt from your mouth whenever you're having fun. Makes it hard to have fun.

Fun fact: when you see 賁 in a kanji, the reading is probably going to be ふん.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 噴き出す (ふきだす) - 噴 means <kanji>eruption</kanji>, and 出す can mean "to let out," right? Well if you let out an eruption, it's probably going to cause something <vocabulary>to burst out</vocabulary>. You know, like lava out of a volcano. Or maybe it's going to <vocabulary>to spout out</vocabulary>, like a geyser out of the earth. Don't be a <reading>foo</reading>l (ふ). This may remind you of another word you've learned: <reading>吹き出す</reading>. They're very similar and often interchangeable, but in general 噴き出す is used for things that spout out with even more power and intensity. Along those lines, it can also be used figuratively, like when pent-up emotions burst out suddenly.

visually_similar_kanji: 爪, 瓜, 弧, 狐
meaning_mnemonic:
There was once a <radical>melon</radical> <radical>child</radical>, that is, a child with the body of a melon. When he was born, his parents didn't want him, so he became an <kanji>orphan</kanji>.

The "melon boy orphan," is what they called him. Imagine a melon (your favorite kind) with a face and arms and legs sticking out. He walks up to you and says "hello kind person, I am an orphan."
reading_mnemonic: The <kanji>orphan</kanji> melon boy is but a <reading>子</reading> (こ).

meaning_mnemonic:
If you give a <radical>machine</radical> a <radical>heart</radical> it will get <kanji>lazy</kanji>. Hearts give us emotions and with emotions we become weak. Why would a machine with a heart want to work anymore? Nah. It's lazy time now.

Picture a machine with a heart, lying on the couch, eating oil snacks, and snoozing. What a lazy machine!
reading_mnemonic:
The machine is so <kanji>lazy</kanji> it won't even wear its <reading>tie</reading> (たい) anymore. That was the only official thing left about it, but now it's as lazy as a human. Would a lazy human put on a tie? I don't think so.

Picture the lazy machine sitting on the couch again. There are untied ties all over the floor.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 怠る (おこたる) - The kanji itself means neglect, so the verb version is to be negligent or to neglect something. If you always seem to be negligent to your kids you'll end up with this situation. It's winter and your kid comes home from school covered in snow and sneezing. "Oh, coat... (おこた)" you say. You didn't give them a coat when they went out today. Maybe if you weren't so negligent that wouldn't have happened. 怠ける (なまける) - The kanji itself means neglect and lazy, so the verb version is to neglect or to be idle. You decide to neglect everything. Your school, your family, even your own name (なま). You've managed to slack for so long that you can't even remember your name? That's pretty impressive, actually. 怠い (だるい) - What's the adjective form of lazy? It's sluggish and dull. The reading for this word is an EXCEPTION. If you're feeling sluggish just turn on Darude's (だる) "Sandstorm" and it will perk you right up. But a world where people don't know Darude's "Sandstorm" is full of sluggish, dull nerds. The machine with a heart doesn't wear its tie, but it wears it's Oh coat (a coat shaped as an O). It forgets it's name, so it says it is Darude from Sandstorm.

meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>soul</radical> is like the <radical>ground</radical> or the <radical>dawn</radical>. It is <kanji>constant</kanji>, never changing.
reading_mnemonic: Also <kanji>constant</kanji> is the Emperor <reading>こう</reading>いち, who will surely rule for a thousand more years! A constant rule from Emperor こういち means constant kanji learning and reviews. They will always be constant!

radical_characters: 忄, ナ, 工, 月
meaning_mnemonic:
In its <radical>soul</radical>, a <radical>narwhal</radical> that's supposed to do <radical>construction</radical> under the <radical>moon</radical>, will be too <kanji>lazy</kanji> to do it. And when your soul is lazy, there's no way you'll be able to get something done.

Picture the lazy narwhal laying on a block of ice in the moonlight. There are tools and other blocks of ice around, but he just can't seem to get up and do any construction work.
reading_mnemonic: You can't tell the <kanji>lazy</kanji> narwhal he's being lazy because he's your <reading>da</reading>d (だ). If he was anyone else you'd tell him off for being lazy, but you can't tell off your dad. That's just not right.

radical_characters: 忄, 日, 罒, 又
meaning_mnemonic:
If your <radical>soul</radical> is acting like the <radical>sun</radical> trapped in a <radical>net</radical> sitting on a <radical>stool</radical>, then people will <kanji>ridicule</kanji> you for your <kanji>laziness</kanji>. You're just sitting there, trapped and not moving.

Your soul just doesn't want to move or do anything though... and that may look like laziness, but you can't help it. You wish your friends and family wouldn't ridicule you. You're going through enough, internally.
reading_mnemonic:
When people <kanji>ridicule</kanji> you, when you can't stop the <kanji>laziness</kanji>, you read <reading>man</reading>ga (まん). Manga helps you feel better about the mean things people say. Manga helps you feel like you're doing something, and that you aren't just a lazy person.

Picture yourself reading manga and watch as the people who ridicule you and call you lazy fade away into the background. You're going to be okay.

radical_characters: 扌, 亠, 幺, 隹
meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>fingers</radical> grasp this <radical>lid</radical> and when you raise it you see a (weird) <radical>poop</radical> <radical>turkey</radical> (a turkey covered in poop). You can't help yourself, you <kanji>embrace</kanji> the turkey.
reading_mnemonic: As you <kanji>embrace</kanji> the sad turkey it makes a funny sound and suddenly starts pooping <reading>yo</reading>gurt (よう) all over you. But you don't want to stop embracing it! It's probably just scared still. But the more you squeeze, the faster the yogurt comes out of it!

meaning_mnemonic:
Within the <radical>yakuza</radical>, having a <radical>slide</radical> on your <radical>jet</radical> means you're <kanji>especially</kanji> important and powerful. It's a symbol of how especially awesome and badass you are.

A jet with a teeter-totter? Normal yakuza boss. A jet with a jungle gym? Powerful yakuza boss. A jet with a slide? Especially powerful yakuza boss.
reading_mnemonic: These <kanji>especially</kanji> powerful yakuza bosses have slides that are like <reading>chu</reading>tes (しゅ) — they're especially fast and especially fun! Just don't get on the bad side of one of these especially important yakuza bosses — a trap door at the bottom of the chute will open and drop you out of their jet.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 殊に (ことに) - What do you wear when it's <vocabulary>especially</vocabulary> cold out? Your favorite <reading>coat</reading> (こと). You only wear it when it's <vocabulary>unusually</vocabulary> cold though, never any other time. Also when you're sliding down the yakuza slide jet, the sky is cold!

kunyomi: おぼ, しず, ない
meaning_mnemonic:
If you figure out how to use a <radical>tsunami</radical> as a <radical>weapon</radical>, everyone is going to <kanji>die</kanji>. You can't control a tsunami, you fool. Now you've doomed us all.

Picture everyone in the world being swept away in a tsunami to die. This is what happens when you try to use nature as a weapon.
reading_mnemonic: The only way to maybe not <kanji>die</kanji> is to find <reading>boats</reading> (ぼつ). As long as the boats don't get smashed by the tsunami, you might be able to cheat death by holding onto the boats and not drowning. You don't want to die, do you? Get to the boats!

meaning_mnemonic: If you take a <radical>cow</radical>'s <radical>life</radical> you're turning it into an <kanji>offering</kanji>. In the old days, cows' lives were given to the gods as offerings pretty often.
reading_mnemonic:
You prepare the <kanji>offering</kanji> with your holy blue <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい). Normally this would be gruesome, but your saber glows and the cow's life shoots up into the sky without you laying a hand on it.

Thanks to the mercy of your saber, the offering is quick and painless. A normal saber, however, would have cut that cow to bits. Like, really just wrecked it. Good thing we didn't have to do that, right?

meaning_mnemonic: There is an <radical>animal</radical> in the <radical>grass</radical> and your (weird) horrible <radical>task</radical> is to go <kanji>hunting</kanji> for it.
reading_mnemonic:
You're currently <kanji>hunting</kanji> in a <reading>row</reading> (りょう) boat and you have to row as quietly and carefully as you can or the animal will run away.

You wouldn't be able to go hunting in any other kind of boat—the motor would be too loud. Picture yourself in a row boat with all of your hunting gear. You need to be extra careful not to make any loud splashing sounds with the oars!

kunyomi: きざ, さいわ, つまび, よ
meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>spirit</radical> of a <radical>sheep</radical> makes it one of the most <kanji>auspicious</kanji> ("showing promise of success and prosperity") creature on the planet. Lights shine out of it and the whole world weeps at its beauty. Look at the sheep's fluffy glowing head. Nothing could be more auspicious and glorious than this.
reading_mnemonic: The spirit sheep is so <kanji>auspicious</kanji> that the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう) declares this day to be the most auspicious of all days. The day when the spirit sheep appeared.

meaning_mnemonic:

meaning_mnemonic:
Under the <radical>moon</radical>, play your <radical>drum</radical> and your <radical>hair</radical> will <kanji>swell</kanji>! The more you play and the longer it's under the moon, the larger your hair will swell.

Have you been suffering from flat, boring hair? Well do I have the swelling treatment you've been looking for!

If someone is rude to you, dish it right back out. F@#$ that guy!

meaning_mnemonic: If a bunch of <radical>flowers</radical> are moving in the same <radical>direction</radical>, you'll be able to smell their <kanji>aromatic</kanji> <kanji>fragrance</kanji>. The best way to bask in their fragrance is to feel the wind that is blowing them in same direction (preferably straight at you). Smells good!
reading_mnemonic: You decide to bring this <kanji>aromatic</kanji> <kanji>fragrance</kanji> into your <reading>ho</reading>me (ほう). To do this, you plant flowers all the way around your home, all facing in toward it.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
芳しい (かんばしい) - The kanji is <kanji>aromatic</kanji>, so this also means <vocabulary>aromatic</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>fragrant</vocabulary>. But be careful if it's a can. Fragrant <reading>can</reading>s will <reading>baa</reading> (かんば) like a sheep at you when you open them. That can baa is just a sweet smell side effect.

芳しい is a formal word, often used in writing to describe <vocabulary>sweet-smelling</vocabulary> flowers, tea, or incense. In a figurative sense it can mean "favorable," too, but this meaning mostly appears in the negative form 芳しくない (unfavorable, poorly received).

meaning_mnemonic:
If you look at <radical>flowers</radical> the first thing you notice are the leaves and petals themselves, then the <radical>next</radical> thing you notice are the <kanji>briar</kanji>s. You never see <kanji>thorn</kanji>s first, only after you've looked at the flowers.

Imagine what you see next after looking at the pretty flowers. The briars are what you see next. Spiky and sharp. It would have been nice if you had seen them first.
reading_mnemonic: When you see the <kanji>briar</kanji>s you can't help but yell, <reading>Eee! Ba ri ars</reading>! (いばら)! You sound funny because you prick your finger on one while you're yelling. Ouch!

meaning_mnemonic:
All you need are some <radical>flowers</radical>, <radical>fish</radical>, and <radical>grain</radical> and you've got yourself a potion that can <kanji>revive</kanji> just about anyone or anything!

Just don't forget the ingredients you'll need: flowers, fish, and grain. Imagine yourself throwing them all into a big cauldron and brewing up a potion powerful enough to revive a person!
reading_mnemonic:
This potion able to <kanji>revive</kanji> any being just has one small downside: it tastes like <reading>so</reading>ap (そ).

As long as you can get over the awful taste of soap, this is some good, powerful stuff! And considering this'll be administered to dead things… the taste is probably not so important.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
蘇る (よみがえる) -  The kanji itself means <kanji>revive</kanji>, but in this case you're the one getting revived, so this means <vocabulary>to be resurrected</vocabulary>. The person you most want <vocabulary>to be resurrected</vocabulary> is the <reading>読み-guy</reading> (よみがえ) — the guy who teaches you the readings of difficult kanji. He died from overwork after you asked him too many kanji readings, so you really want him <vocabulary>to come back to life</vocabulary> and help you study some more. Have this yomi-guy drink your soap-flavored potion.

Alternatively, you can remember this as <reading>黄泉(よみ) + 帰る</reading>: coming home from the land of the dead. Just don't forget the rendaku on 帰る!

蘇る is a dramatic-sounding word for something coming back to life. It can be literal (yes, even zombies), but it's also used for figurative resurrections, like being vividly reminded of an old memory.

Fun fact: the word originally means "to return from 黄泉(よみ)," the land of the dead in Japanese mythology. That's why 蘇る sounds so dramatic — it makes you think of someone returning from the underworld to the mortal world!

meaning_mnemonic: Take a <radical>leather</radical> <radical>helicopter</radical> to the <radical>moon</radical> to prove your excellent <kanji>leadership</kanji>. Some people called you crazy, but you'll show them, as you lead an entire crew of leather helicopter pilots on their first mission to space! reading_mnemonic:
Under your superior <kanji>leadership</kanji> you and your leather helicopter crew are able to make it to the moon. The moon! Your crew is so impressed by your leadership, and their lack of being very dead, and they all start laughing, "<reading>Ha</reading> (は) ha ha ha!" They thought they were going to die but you lead them to the moon safely!

Imagine laughing along with the crew, in awe at your own leadership skills. Ha ha ha! We're alive!

貫く is a relatively formal word, mostly used in writing. It can mean physically piercing something, but more often it means <vocabulary>to follow through</vocabulary> on your beliefs or goals all the way to the end.

meaning_mnemonic:
You give a bunch of <radical>shellfish</radical> to a <radical>clown</radical> as <kanji>compensation</kanji>. The clown did you some favors, and everyone knows clowns only accept shellfish as a form of currency. So your compensation is a pile of random shellfish.

Once the clown has been properly <kanji>compensate</kanji>d, he looks you in the eyes, one hand full of shellfish, the other in the air, and waves, "<reading>Bye</reading> (ばい)" he says. "Bye, bye."

All you have to do is give him the right amount of compensation and you'll hear his sweet "bye, bye." Then you never have to see him again.

meaning_mnemonic:
Your poor little <radical>scooter</radical> got a <radical>splinter</radical>, so make sure to give it extra nice <kanji>treatment</kanji>. These are tough times for your scooter, so be patient with it. Try to treat it with understanding and care.

Also, when this means "treatment," note that it doesn't refer to medical treatment, but rather about how you personally treat or receive people.

The long vowel is important here, so try to think of different ways you could make your scooter feel gooooood. Maybe a nice little wash after you’ve removed the splinter will do the trick.

They're all coming out to meet you, pulling back their skin and showing you the soul ghosts inside of them. "We love your music, look at our souls!" Uh oh, this is turning into some kind of horror movie. You better scoot a bit faster.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 遭う (あう) - Remember how 会う also means <vocabulary>to meet</vocabulary>? Well they're both read あう too! So if you know that one, you know this one too! 遭う can also be <vocabulary>to encounter</vocabulary>.

They link their triceratops horns together and form an unbreakable gold chain. You can't eat them, because they're gold. So they're only really good for their chaining together ability.

Picture these little gold triceratops shellfish linked together by their horns in a chain around your neck. Feel them hanging there. Sparkly and cold.
reading_mnemonic:
However, the only way to break the <kanji>chain</kanji> is to cut it open with a <reading>saw</reading> (さ). Once the golden triceratops shellfish start holding on, they never let go. So when you want to take the chain off you have to really hack at it with your saw.

Picture the saw in your hands, sawing back and forth on the gold chain around your neck. Maybe this isn't the best fashion accessory if you have to use a saw to get it off.
extra_reading_mnemonic: 鎖 (くさり) - The best way to break out of the <vocabulary>chains</vocabulary> life puts on you is to put on a <reading>cool sari</reading> (くさり). A cool sari will remind you where you come from. Who your family is. And how beautiful you look. Cast off those chains and put on a cool sari!

You see, prisons aren't built very carefully, they just try to get them done fast enough to stuff people in there. So while you can tell this was once a building, it definitely isn't a prison anymore, since the whole thing caved in.
reading_mnemonic:
You keep picturing the <kanji>cave in</kanji> and you see Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん) climbing over the rubble. He's the one who took down this prison! And he's coming for your town next!

Genghis Khan is all about being smart and using better tactics. In this case, why fight a bunch of guards and prisoners when you can just cause a cave in and win immediately? The ol' Khan cave in, a classic war maneuver.
extra_reading_mnemonic:
陥る (おちいる) - The kanji itself means <kanji>cave in</kanji>, and the verb version takes that feeling further. It means <vocabulary>to fall into</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be thrown into</vocabulary> something negative, like a trap, trouble, or even a bad emotional state. Whenever you're about <vocabulary>to fall into</vocabulary> a physical or emotional pit of doom, you just mutter, "<reading>Oh chee</reading>se <reading>ea</reading>tery (おちい)..." Because that's where it always starts. You can never resist the temptations of their mysterious fondue. Oh, that cheese eatery is like a trap for people with no self-control. Get ahold of yourself! Your life is falling into cheesy ruin!!

陥る describes a moment when the world around you or your heart caves in, and you're suddenly thrown into that space and get trapped inside. It's like slipping into a dark hole in life you didn't see coming. That's the feeling!
